legend.label: Tier 3 — the desks that page you

roles.name: Identity engineer
roles.definition: You work the sign-in plane: tokens, factors, eligible assignments, the quiet accumulation of standing rights nobody reviews. Nights on your watch tilt toward stolen credentials and privilege that outlived its reason, because that is the traffic you can actually read.

roles.name: Data and network engineer
roles.definition: You work where the data sits and how it travels: account keys and signatures, public endpoints, firewall rules, the private link somebody never finished. Your nights tilt toward exposure that was configured, not breached.

roles.name: AI security lead
roles.definition: You work the newest and least settled surface: agents with their own identities, copilots with reach into everything their user can see, models behind gateways. Your nights tilt toward blast radius — what an agent could touch, not what it did.

roles.name: Detection engineer
roles.definition: You work the telemetry: what is collected, what it costs, what fires and what stays quiet. Your nights tilt toward the gap between an event happening and anyone finding out.

cards.q: At a regional hospital trust, the on-call messaging engineer requests activation of her eligible Exchange Administrator assignment at 02:10 to clear a stuck transport queue. The role is configured to require approval, and the single named approver is asleep. She resubmits twice overnight and the ticket is still pending when the day shift arrives 28 hours later. What change to the PIM role setting stops this recurring?
options: Name two or more delegated approvers on the role, because a pending activation request expires after 24 hours and that window cannot be lengthened
Raise the maximum activation duration for the role from two hours to eight hours so the request stays open longer
Switch the engineer from a permanent eligible assignment to a permanent active assignment for Exchange Administrator
Turn on the PIM weekly digest email so approvers are reminded of outstanding activation requests
cards.answer: Name two or more delegated approvers on the role, because a pending activation request expires after 24 hours and that window cannot be lengthened
cards.why: PIM gives delegated approvers 24 hours to act; after that the eligible user has to submit a fresh request, and the 24-hour window is not a configurable setting, so the only real fix is more approvers on the rota. The nearest wrong answer, raising the maximum activation duration, controls how long the role stays usable once it is activated, not how long the approval request survives, so the request would still lapse unanswered.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra PIM docs: approving role activation requests; PIM deployment planning · outline 1.1

cards.q: A retail bank's external auditor asks for evidence of every privileged role activation over the past twelve months. The identity team opens Privileged Identity Management, selects Microsoft Entra roles, and finds the Resource audit view returns nothing older than a month no matter which custom date range they pick. What should have been configured so the twelve months of evidence existed?
options: Diagnostic settings routing the Microsoft Entra sign-in and audit logs into Azure storage via Azure Monitor, because PIM audit history itself only holds the past 30 days
A recurring access review on each privileged role, which preserves activation history for the review period
The My audit view instead of Resource audit, which retains a longer history per individual administrator
PIM security alerts for Microsoft Entra roles, which archive every activation event they evaluate
cards.answer: Diagnostic settings routing the Microsoft Entra sign-in and audit logs into Azure storage via Azure Monitor, because PIM audit history itself only holds the past 30 days
cards.why: PIM keeps audit data for 30 days and no longer; retaining it beyond that means shipping the Microsoft Entra logs into Azure storage using Azure Monitor before the evidence ages out. Access reviews are the closest tempting answer because they do generate a decision record, but they attest to whether an assignment is still needed rather than logging each individual activation, so they cannot reconstruct a year of role elevations.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra PIM docs: role audit history; archiving Entra logs with Azure Monitor · outline 1.1

cards.q: A university identity engineer edits the Conditional Access policy that protects the research grants application. It currently uses the grant control Require multifactor authentication. She ticks Require authentication strength and picks the built-in Phishing-resistant MFA strength, leaving the MFA checkbox ticked as well, then tries to save. What is the correct configuration?
options: Clear the Require multifactor authentication checkbox and leave Require authentication strength alone, because those two grant controls cannot be combined in one policy
Keep both controls and switch the policy to Require one of the selected controls so either will satisfy it
Keep both controls and leave the default Require all the selected controls, which layers the strength on top of MFA
Replace the built-in strength with a custom authentication strength, which is the only kind that can sit alongside Require multifactor authentication
cards.answer: Clear the Require multifactor authentication checkbox and leave Require authentication strength alone, because those two grant controls cannot be combined in one policy
cards.why: Require multifactor authentication and Require authentication strength are unsupported together in the same policy, since the built-in Multifactor authentication strength is the exact equivalent of the MFA grant control. Choosing Require one of the selected controls is the nearest miss and is actively harmful reasoning: the restriction is on the pairing itself, not on the and/or combination logic, and an or would in any case let a weak password-plus-SMS sign-in through the door you were trying to harden.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra docs: Conditional Access authentication strengths; CA grant controls · outline 1.1

cards.q: A grocery retailer is shutting the door on basic authentication to Exchange Online. The security lead builds a Conditional Access policy assigned to Exchange Online with the grant control set to Block access, and now has to set the client apps condition so it catches POP, IMAP, SMTP AUTH and older Outlook profiles but leaves the Outlook mobile app and Outlook on the web working. Which selection does that?
options: Under client apps, select Exchange ActiveSync clients and Other clients only
Under client apps, select Browser and Mobile apps and desktop clients only
Leave client apps unconfigured, because a new policy applies to all client app types by default
Add a Filter for devices condition that excludes devices with a trustType of Microsoft Entra joined
cards.answer: Under client apps, select Exchange ActiveSync clients and Other clients only
cards.why: The legacy authentication client types are Exchange ActiveSync clients and Other clients, and Other clients is the bucket holding SMTP, IMAP4, POP3, MAPI over HTTP, EWS, Autodiscover and Offline Address Book. Leaving the condition unconfigured is the trap: it is true that a new policy covers all client app types by default, but paired with Block access that would take out browsers and modern desktop clients too and shut the retailer out of its own mailboxes.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra docs: Conditional Access conditions, client apps · outline 1.1

cards.q: A contract manufacturer is about to switch on a policy that blocks access from any device platform other than Windows, iOS and Android. Roughly 4,000 staff and an unknown number of shop-floor kiosks are in scope, and the change board wants proof of real-world impact before enforcement, not a hypothesis. What does the identity team do first?
options: Save the policy in report-only mode, run it for at least a week, and read the Report-only tab on individual events in the sign-in logs
Run the What If tool against a sample of representative user accounts and applications and attach the output to the change record
Enable the policy for a pilot group of 50 users and watch the Conditional Access Coverage tab for seven days
Enable the policy tenant-wide out of hours and rely on disabling it if the service desk call volume spikes
cards.answer: Save the policy in report-only mode, run it for at least a week, and read the Report-only tab on individual events in the sign-in logs
cards.why: Report-only mode evaluates the policy against genuine sign-in traffic and records what would have happened without denying anyone, and Microsoft's guidance is to run each policy that way for at least a week before enforcing it. The What If tool is the closest wrong answer and is a fine companion, but it simulates a sign-in you describe by hand, so it only ever tells you about the scenarios you thought to type in, which is exactly the blind spot with unknown kiosks.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra docs: planning a CA deployment; CA report-only mode · outline 1.1

cards.q: An insurer's identity administrator disables text message as an authentication method in the Authentication methods policy for everyone. A fortnight later, sampling shows several hundred staff still completing verification by SMS and, in some cases, by voice call. The tenant has not been touched since. Why is this happening?
options: Those users are still enabled for the method in a legacy policy, and a method stays usable while any policy permits it
The Authentication methods policy exceeded 20 KB when saved, so the disable operation was silently dropped
Text message can only be disabled per group, and a tenant-wide disable is ignored for users who already registered the method
The users have not signed out, so their existing refresh tokens carry the old method entitlement until they expire
cards.answer: Those users are still enabled for the method in a legacy policy, and a method stays usable while any policy permits it
cards.why: Settings are not synchronised between the Authentication methods policy, the legacy MFA policy and the legacy SSPR policy, and Microsoft Entra ID honours all three, so a method has to be disabled everywhere to be gone. That also explains the voice calls: the legacy SSPR Mobile phone option turns on text message and voice together. The 20 KB answer is a real limit and therefore tempting, but it blocks the save outright when a policy targets too many groups rather than quietly discarding one method.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra docs: managing authentication methods, how the policies interact · outline 1.1

cards.q: A logistics firm onboards drivers in depot batches. Each new starter gets a single-use Temporary Access Pass, joins their Windows laptop to Microsoft Entra ID, and is then meant to register a passkey. Device join reliably takes 20 to 30 minutes over depot Wi-Fi, and the passkey step fails every time, sending the driver back to the depot lead for another pass. What should the identity team change?
options: Turn off one-time use in the Temporary Access Pass policy so a single pass can be reused across the join and the credential registration
Raise the Temporary Access Pass maximum lifetime setting towards its ceiling of 43,200 minutes
Increase the Temporary Access Pass length from 8 characters to 48 characters to reduce mistyped passes
Exclude the driver onboarding group from Conditional Access so no policy interrupts the registration
cards.answer: Turn off one-time use in the Temporary Access Pass policy so a single pass can be reused across the join and the credential registration
cards.why: Registering a passwordless method after signing in with a one-time pass has to be completed within 10 minutes, and that ten-minute clock is an MFA-during-registration rule, not something the pass lifetime governs. A multi-use pass sidesteps it because the timer effectively restarts when the user begins registering the new method. Extending the maximum lifetime is the near miss: it keeps the pass valid for longer but does nothing to the 10-minute registration limit that is actually failing.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra docs: Temporary Access Pass policy and passwordless registration · outline 1.1

cards.q: A university developer tidying the tenant deletes the app registration for the timetabling web app, realises the mistake an hour later, and restores the application object from the deleted applications list in App registrations. The client ID is intact and the secret is still there, yet every sign-in to the app now fails. What is going on?
options: Restoring the application object does not restore its home-tenant service principal, and without that enterprise application entry no one can sign in
The client secret was invalidated on deletion and has to be reissued even though it is still listed
The redirect URI is dropped on restore and has to be re-added to the app registration
The application object was recreated with a new object ID, so all existing token-issuing trust is broken
cards.answer: Restoring the application object does not restore its home-tenant service principal, and without that enterprise application entry no one can sign in
cards.why: Deleting an application object also deletes the service principal in its home tenant, and restoring the application through the App registrations experience brings back only the application object, so the local identity the tenant actually authenticates and authorises against is missing. Reissuing the client secret is the closest wrong answer and a natural reflex, but a fresh credential on an application object with no service principal still has nothing to sign in as. For a planned pause, deactivating the application preserves both objects instead.
cards.citation: Microsoft identity platform docs: application objects and service principals · outline 1.1

cards.q: A supermarket chain currently lets every employee consent to any application for permissions that do not need an administrator. The CISO wants that narrowed without stopping buyers and store managers from adopting small productivity tools on their own. Which configuration meets both halves of that brief?
options: Assign microsoft-user-default-low as the user consent policy, and classify the specific delegated permissions you are willing to allow as low impact
Assign microsoft-user-default-legacy as the user consent policy, which limits consent to apps registered in your own tenant
Remove all user consent permission grant policies so only administrators can consent, and tell staff to raise a ticket
Require user assignment on every enterprise application so only assigned users can consent to it
cards.answer: Assign microsoft-user-default-low as the user consent policy, and classify the specific delegated permissions you are willing to allow as low impact
cards.why: The microsoft-user-default-low policy lets staff consent only where the app comes from a verified publisher or is registered in your own tenant, and only to delegated permissions you have classified as low impact, which is precisely the narrowed-but-not-closed posture asked for. The legacy built-in policy is the trap because its name suggests restriction: in fact it lets any user consent to whatever permission does not need an administrator, in any application, which is the setting they already have.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra docs: user consent configuration; permission classifications · outline 1.1

cards.q: An electronics manufacturer runs a nightly burst of ephemeral build agents: several hundred virtual machines created and destroyed inside a couple of hours, all needing read access to the same Azure Storage account. The platform team also insists the storage permission exists before any VM is deployed, and the engineers who deploy the VMs are not allowed to create role assignments. What identity design fits?
options: One user-assigned managed identity, created and granted the storage role in advance, then attached to every build agent
A system-assigned managed identity turned on for every build VM, with the storage role granted at first boot
A single app registration whose client secret lives in Azure Key Vault and is read by each agent at start-up
A system-assigned managed identity on each VM, all added to one Microsoft Entra security group that holds the storage role
cards.answer: One user-assigned managed identity, created and granted the storage role in advance, then attached to every build agent
cards.why: A user-assigned identity has a lifecycle independent of the compute, so its role assignment can be made ahead of deployment and the deployers only need permission to attach it; it also avoids the Microsoft Entra object creation rate limit that rapid system-assigned identity churn can trip, which surfaces as HTTP 429. The security-group variant is the closest wrong answer and fails for a subtler reason: group and role membership travels as claims in a token, and managed identity tokens are cached by the back-end for around 24 hours, so membership changes take hours to bite.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra docs: managed identity best practices; managed identities overview · outline 1.1

cards.q: 03:12. A hospital's PIM alert fires: a helpdesk analyst's account, eligible for Privileged Role Administrator, activated the role four minutes ago from an unfamiliar IP and is already creating permanent active assignments for two unknown accounts. The analyst is asleep and confirms by phone she did nothing. The role is live right now. What is your containment move?
options: As a Global Administrator, remove the active role assignment in PIM and revoke the account's sessions, then unpick the assignments it created
Edit the role setting to require approval on activation so the attacker cannot elevate again
Delete the analyst's eligible assignment for Privileged Role Administrator
Open Discovery and insights and run Eliminate standing access across the tenant's privileged roles
cards.answer: As a Global Administrator, remove the active role assignment in PIM and revoke the account's sessions, then unpick the assignments it created
cards.why: A Global Administrator or Privileged Role Administrator can remove the active assignment of a user who should not be active, which is the only one of these that ends privilege that is already in use; revoking sessions stops the token in the attacker's hand being replayed. Requiring approval is the closest wrong answer and is the right hardening later, but role settings govern the next activation, not the live one, and the attacker keeps working while you save the policy. Deleting the eligible assignment has the same flaw and can be refused outright, since an assignment cannot be removed within five minutes of being made.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra PIM docs: role assignment and the approval workflow · outline 1.1

cards.q: A challenger bank's sign-in logs are lighting up: tens of thousands of password attempts an hour against staff accounts, sourced from countries where the bank has no staff, no offices and no customers. A handful of accounts have already had a correct password accepted. You need a Conditional Access change on the bridge in the next ten minutes. What do you enable?
options: A policy targeting all users and all resources that blocks access from any network location, with a named location listing the countries you operate in set as the exclusion, and your emergency access accounts excluded
A policy that adds the attacking IP ranges to a named location and marks that location as trusted so the sign-ins are flagged for review
A policy that turns off resilience defaults for all users so sessions cannot be extended during the incident
Security defaults for the tenant, which enforce multifactor authentication registration for every user immediately
cards.answer: A policy targeting all users and all resources that blocks access from any network location, with a named location listing the countries you operate in set as the exclusion, and your emergency access accounts excluded
cards.why: Building an allowed-countries named location and blocking everything else is the documented pattern for organisations with a small geographic footprint, and it collapses the attack surface in one policy rather than chasing IP ranges. Excluding the emergency access accounts is not optional; they must sit outside every policy or you can lock yourself out mid-incident. Marking the attacker ranges as trusted is the nearest wrong answer and inverts the control: trusted locations relax requirements rather than deny, so it would help the attacker.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra docs: planning a CA deployment, named locations and emergency access · outline 1.1

cards.q: A multi-academy trust's Defender alert names an application called Mail Archive Helper. Forty-one staff consented to it themselves over the weekend; it holds delegated Mail.Read and Files.Read.All and is pulling mailbox content right now. It is a multitenant app, so nothing exists for it under App registrations. In the Entra admin center the Permissions blade shows the grants on the User consent tab with no way to revoke them. What do you do to stop the exfiltration?
options: Delete the application's oAuth2PermissionGrant objects with Microsoft Graph or PowerShell and disable user sign-in to the enterprise application
Revoke the permissions from the Admin consent tab of the application's Permissions blade in the Entra admin center
Change the tenant user consent setting to admin-only, which withdraws the consent the forty-one users already gave
Delete the application object from App registrations so the service principal is removed with it
cards.answer: Delete the application's oAuth2PermissionGrant objects with Microsoft Graph or PowerShell and disable user sign-in to the enterprise application
cards.why: Grants shown on the User consent tab cannot be revoked from the portal at all; removing them means deleting the oAuth2PermissionGrant objects through Microsoft Graph or the equivalent PowerShell cmdlets, and disabling user sign-in to the app stops it acquiring anything new. The Admin consent tab is the closest wrong answer and is the one place the portal does let you revoke, but it only covers grants an administrator made for the whole organisation, which is not what happened here. Tightening the consent setting is worth doing afterwards and changes nothing today, because it affects only future consent operations.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra docs: reviewing permissions granted to enterprise apps; user consent configuration · outline 1.1

cards.q: A fashion retailer's developer account has been taken over. The attacker has editing rights on a Logic App that carries a user-assigned managed identity, and that identity is a member of a Microsoft Entra security group holding Storage Blob Data Contributor on the customer-orders storage account. Runs are firing every ninety seconds and blobs are moving. Your colleague is already removing the identity from the security group. What do you tell them?
options: Removing it from the group will not stop this in time, because managed identity tokens are cached for around 24 hours; strip the role assignment held directly on the identity and detach the identity from the Logic App
Removing it from the group is the right move, and access will drop as soon as the current one-hour access token expires
Delete the user-assigned managed identity, which removes its role assignments along with it
Disable the compromised developer account, which revokes the tokens the managed identity has already been issued
cards.answer: Removing it from the group will not stop this in time, because managed identity tokens are cached for around 24 hours; strip the role assignment held directly on the identity and detach the identity from the Logic App
cards.why: Group and role membership arrives as claims inside the access token, and the back-end services for managed identities keep a per-resource cache for roughly 24 hours with no way to force a refresh, so a group removal can take hours to take effect. Acting on the role assignment held directly by the identity, and pulling the identity off the Logic App, cuts the path now. The one-hour token answer is the near miss: that is human user token behaviour, not the managed identity caching that applies here. Deleting the identity is also wrong on its own terms, since role assignments are not removed automatically when a managed identity is deleted.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra docs: managed identity best practices, authorization caching limits · outline 1.1

cards.q: After the overnight privileged-role incident, the hospital's identity board sits down to fix the standing-privilege problem properly. Discovery and insights shows eleven accounts permanently active in Global Administrator, including two cloud-only accounts the team keeps for emergencies. What should the target state be?
options: Convert the nine working administrators to eligible assignments requiring MFA, justification and approval with a one-hour activation, and leave the two emergency access accounts permanently active and excluded from Conditional Access
Convert all eleven accounts, emergency accounts included, to eligible assignments requiring MFA and approval, so no account holds standing privilege
Leave the assignments active but add a quarterly access review on the Global Administrator role and rely on the reviewers to trim it
Convert the nine working administrators to time-bound active assignments with a three-month end date so they expire on their own
cards.answer: Convert the nine working administrators to eligible assignments requiring MFA, justification and approval with a one-hour activation, and leave the two emergency access accounts permanently active and excluded from Conditional Access
cards.why: Microsoft's deployment guidance is zero permanently active assignments for every role except the emergency access accounts, with Global Administrator protected by MFA, justification, approval and a short activation window. Putting the emergency accounts behind PIM as well is the closest wrong answer and is the classic self-inflicted outage, since those accounts exist precisely for when activation, approval or MFA is what has failed. Time-bound active assignments are also wrong here: the privilege still stands for three months, the only thing that expires is the assignment.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra PIM docs: deployment planning; Discovery and insights for Entra roles · outline 1.1

cards.q: Reviewing the consent incident, the trust finds a second issue. Six weeks ago an administrator granted tenant-wide admin consent to a legitimate pharmacy stock application so the twelve pharmacy staff would stop seeing consent prompts, and every one of the trust's 4,000 accounts has been able to open it ever since. The application itself is trusted and is staying. What should have been done alongside the admin consent?
options: Set the enterprise application to require user assignment, then assign only the pharmacy group
Set the enterprise application's Visible to users property to No so it is hidden from the My Apps portal
Deactivate the application between pharmacy shifts so tokens are only issued while it is in use
Grant consent on behalf of each of the twelve pharmacy staff individually instead of tenant-wide
cards.answer: Set the enterprise application to require user assignment, then assign only the pharmacy group
cards.why: Tenant-wide admin consent lets every user in the organisation reach the app unless you restrict it, and the documented restriction is to require user assignment on the application and then assign the users or groups that should have it. Hiding the app from My Apps is the closest wrong answer because it looks like it limits reach, but visibility is cosmetic: anyone with a direct link or the client itself can still sign in, so the exposure is unchanged.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra docs: tenant-wide admin consent; evaluating application consent requests · outline 1.1

cards.q: A payments processor is standing up a vault for the keys that wrap its card-tokenisation database. The regulator's control text says the private key material must be generated inside, and must never leave, an HSM validated to FIPS 140-3 Level 3. The team wants an ordinary key vault resource, not a dedicated pool. How should the vault and its keys be created?
options: Create the key vault on the Premium tier and create the keys with an HSM-backed key type such as RSA-HSM
Create the key vault on the Standard tier and create RSA keys, then enable purge protection to satisfy the control
Create the key vault on the Standard tier and import the keys from the on-premises HSM using Bring Your Own Key
Create the key vault on the Standard tier and enable Azure Disk Encryption so the keys are hardware protected
cards.answer: Create the key vault on the Premium tier and create the keys with an HSM-backed key type such as RSA-HSM
cards.why: Only the Premium tier offers HSM-protected keys backed by FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated hardware; the Standard tier encrypts using software cryptographic modules validated to FIPS 140 Level 1. The closest wrong answer is the Standard tier with an imported key: importing key material from your own HSM does not change the tier's protection level, and the key still lands in a software-protected slot. Purge protection and disk encryption are unrelated controls and speak to recoverability and workload encryption, not to where key material lives.
cards.citation: About Azure Key Vault (service tiers and HSM protection) · outline 1.2

cards.q: A hospital trust's records-retention standard says deleted cryptographic material must become unrecoverable within 30 days. The platform team already created a production vault six weeks ago and accepted the defaults, so deleted objects linger for 90 days. The compliance lead wants the 30-day figure enforced on this workload. What has to happen?
options: Create a replacement vault with the retention interval set to 30 days at creation and migrate the objects, because the interval is fixed once the vault exists
Update the existing vault's soft-delete retention interval to 30 days with Update-AzKeyVault, then confirm the new value in the portal
Turn soft delete off on the existing vault and turn it back on, choosing 30 days during the re-enable step
Assign an Azure Policy definition that sets the retention interval to 30 days and let the next remediation task correct the vault
cards.answer: Create a replacement vault with the retention interval set to 30 days at creation and migrate the objects, because the interval is fixed once the vault exists
cards.why: The soft-delete retention interval is chosen only at vault creation, may be set anywhere from 7 to 90 days, and cannot be altered afterwards, so a new vault is the only route to a different figure. The tempting wrong answer is the Update cmdlet, which happily changes many vault properties but not this one. Soft delete itself cannot be disabled once on, and Azure Policy can audit or require a setting on new vaults but cannot rewrite an immutable property on an existing one.
cards.citation: Azure Key Vault soft-delete overview (retention policy interval) · outline 1.2

cards.q: A shipping firm's route-planner container app authenticates with its own managed identity and must fetch one partner API token kept in a vault on the Azure RBAC model. Auditors insist it can fetch that value and nothing else — no changing, removing or rotating. What do you grant?
options: Key Vault Secrets User on that vault, so the identity can get secret values and do nothing more
Key Vault Reader on that vault, so the identity can list the token and view its properties
Key Vault Secrets Officer on that vault, so the identity can also refresh the token when it expires
Key Vault Contributor on that vault, so the identity can manage the vault that holds the token
cards.answer: Key Vault Secrets User on that vault, so the identity can get secret values and do nothing more
cards.why: Key Vault Secrets User reads secret contents and nothing more, which is exactly the app's need under least privilege. Key Vault Reader is the nearest trap: it reads metadata about the vault and its objects but deliberately cannot read sensitive values, so the app would enumerate the secret and still fail on retrieval. Secrets Officer adds set and delete rights the app must not have, and Key Vault Contributor is a control-plane role that grants no data access at all.
cards.citation: Key Vault RBAC built-in roles for keys, certificates and secrets · outline 1.2

cards.q: An internal audit at an insurer finds that an application-support engineer holding the Contributor role on the resource group read production secrets last quarter, even though nobody granted them data access. The vault still uses the legacy access policy model. What is the correct remediation?
options: Switch the vault to the Azure RBAC permission model and replace the engineer's Contributor assignment with a narrowly scoped role such as Key Vault Reader
Leave the access policy model in place and remove the engineer's access policy entry, keeping Contributor for deployment work
Replace Contributor with Key Vault Contributor so the engineer keeps deployment rights while losing the ability to read secrets
Enable purge protection and diagnostic logging so any future secret reads are captured for the audit trail
cards.answer: Switch the vault to the Azure RBAC permission model and replace the engineer's Contributor assignment with a narrowly scoped role such as Key Vault Reader
cards.why: Under the access policy model a holder of control-plane Contributor can simply write themselves an access policy and reach the data plane, which is precisely the escalation the audit found; moving the vault to Azure RBAC and trimming the assignment closes it. The near miss is Key Vault Contributor: that role does block data access on its own, but it still carries vault write permission, and while access policies remain the authorization system the escalation path is only narrowed, not removed. Deleting one policy entry leaves the engineer free to recreate it, and logging records the abuse rather than preventing it.
cards.citation: Azure RBAC versus access policies, and the Key Vault Contributor warning · outline 1.2

cards.q: A car-parts manufacturer runs a batch job on virtual machines in a subnet whose outbound public addresses change constantly. The vault holding the job's signing key must reject everything except that subnet, over the public endpoint path. Which configuration works?
options: Enable the Microsoft.KeyVault service endpoint on the subnet, add a virtual network rule for it on the vault, and set the default action to Deny
Add the virtual machines' private addresses in the 10.0.0.0/8 space to the vault's IP rules and set the default action to Deny
Tick the firewall exception that lets trusted Microsoft services skip network rules, since Azure Virtual Machines qualify
Attach a network security group to the subnet that permits outbound traffic to the Key Vault service tag and deny the rest
cards.answer: Enable the Microsoft.KeyVault service endpoint on the subnet, add a virtual network rule for it on the vault, and set the default action to Deny
cards.why: Virtual network rules exist for exactly this case, where the client's public address is dynamic; the service endpoint on the subnet is the prerequisite, and Deny closes everything else. The most seductive wrong option is listing the private addresses: Key Vault IP rules accept public addresses only and explicitly reject RFC 1918 ranges such as 10., 172.16 to 172.31 and 192.168. Trusted-services bypass is a list of Microsoft first-party services, not your own virtual machines, and a network security group filters traffic leaving the subnet without constraining who else may reach the vault.
cards.citation: Configure network security for Azure Key Vault (virtual network rules and IP rule limitations) · outline 1.2

cards.q: A grocery chain turns on the vault firewall and ticks the box allowing trusted Microsoft services to bypass it. Overnight the release pipeline fails: an Azure DevOps Microsoft-hosted agent can no longer pull the deployment secret, although the pipeline's identity holds Key Vault Secrets User. What is the right fix?
options: Move the pipeline to a self-hosted agent in a virtual network that the vault admits through a virtual network rule
Confirm the trusted Microsoft services bypass is saved, since Azure DevOps is admitted once that exception is applied
Grant the pipeline identity Key Vault Administrator so it can read the secret regardless of the firewall
Set public network access on the vault to Disabled, which restores first-party Microsoft connectivity
cards.answer: Move the pipeline to a self-hosted agent in a virtual network that the vault admits through a virtual network rule
cards.why: Azure DevOps is not on the trusted services list, because customers write the code that runs there, so the bypass never admits it and the hosted agent's shifting addresses cannot be allow-listed reliably; a self-hosted agent inside an admitted network solves it, as would a private endpoint. The closest wrong answer is re-checking the bypass, which is the natural assumption but simply does not cover this service. Widening the role misreads a network denial as a permissions denial, and disabling public access tightens the vault further, leaving only trusted services and private endpoints.
cards.citation: Configure network security for Azure Key Vault (trusted services bypass) · outline 1.2

cards.q: A building society uses a vault key as the customer-managed key for a storage account holding statement archives. The security team sets a rotation policy so a new key version appears every 18 months and wants the storage account to move to each new version with no human step and no read failures. What must be true of the configuration?
options: The storage account references the key by its versionless identifier, and the previous key version stays enabled until the service finishes re-wrapping
The storage account references a specific key version, and an automation runbook updates that reference each time the policy fires
The old key version is disabled as soon as the new version is created, so no data can be read under the superseded material
The archives are re-encrypted end to end by the rotation, so once rotation reports success either version may be removed
cards.answer: The storage account references the key by its versionless identifier, and the previous key version stays enabled until the service finishes re-wrapping
cards.why: Zero-touch rotation depends on the target service holding a versionless key URI so it picks up the newest version by itself, and the old version must remain enabled while the service re-wraps its data encryption keys, which can take from an hour to a day or more. The nearest wrong answer, a versioned reference plus a runbook, is a real pattern for services that lack automatic pickup but defeats the point here and reintroduces the manual step. Rotation re-wraps data encryption keys rather than re-encrypting the archives themselves, so disabling the old version early breaks reads.
cards.citation: Azure Key Vault automated key-rotation policy · outline 1.2

cards.q: A regional airline's public booking site went dark last year when a TLS certificate lapsed unnoticed. The platform team now wants the vault to renew the certificate itself and to email the operations mailbox before each lifecycle event. How should they set this up?
options: Create a Key Vault certificate whose policy names an integrated issuer such as DigiCert or GlobalSign with an autoRenew lifetime action, and set certificate contacts on the vault
Upload the PFX as a Key Vault secret and configure a key rotation policy on it so a fresh version is generated before expiry
Import the certificate and rely on Microsoft Defender for Key Vault to alert on the approaching expiry date
Create the certificate as self-signed with an autoRenew action, then have the certificate authority countersign each renewed version
cards.answer: Create a Key Vault certificate whose policy names an integrated issuer such as DigiCert or GlobalSign with an autoRenew lifetime action, and set certificate contacts on the vault
cards.why: Automatic renewal of a publicly trusted certificate needs an issuer object for a partnered certificate authority referenced from the certificate policy, plus an autoRenew lifetime action; certificate contacts are vault-wide and carry the lifecycle notifications. The closest wrong option stores the certificate as a secret, which is expressly discouraged and gets no lifecycle management at all, and key rotation policies apply to keys rather than certificates. Defender for Key Vault raises alerts on anomalous access, not on expiry, and a self-signed certificate cannot be promoted to a CA-issued one by renewal.
cards.citation: About Azure Key Vault certificates (policy, issuers, contacts) · outline 1.2

cards.q: A logistics firm runs workloads in Azure and AWS. After a breach at a peer, its CISO wants agentless discovery of plaintext credentials sitting both on virtual machine disks and inside infrastructure-as-code deployment resources, with the findings surfacing in attack path analysis. Which plan should be enabled?
options: Defender Cloud Security Posture Management, which covers machine scanning as well as cloud deployment resource scanning
Defender for Servers Plan 2, which covers machine secrets scanning and therefore the deployment resources those machines create
Defender for Key Vault, so anomalous access to any discovered credential is alerted on across both clouds
Defender for Storage with malware scanning, which inspects file content at rest for embedded credentials
cards.answer: Defender Cloud Security Posture Management, which covers machine scanning as well as cloud deployment resource scanning
cards.why: Machine secrets scanning is available under either the Defender CSPM plan or under Servers Plan 2, but scanning of cloud deployment resources sits under Defender CSPM alone, so only that plan meets both halves of the requirement, and attack path analysis is a CSPM capability. The near miss is Servers Plan 2, which genuinely delivers the virtual machine half and stops there. Defender for Key Vault watches vault access rather than hunting exposed secrets, and Defender for Storage addresses a different asset entirely.
cards.citation: Protecting secrets in Microsoft Defender for Cloud (scanning types and plans) · outline 1.2

cards.q: A water utility's security operations lead wants alerting on anomalous vault access, such as a service principal that suddenly lists and reads secrets it has never touched, with no agents to deploy and no rules to author. Where is this switched on?
options: In Microsoft Defender for Cloud, open Environment settings, choose the subscription, and toggle the Key Vault plan on
On the key vault itself, open the Security page and enable threat protection for that vault
In the vault's Diagnostic settings, stream AuditEvent logs to a Log Analytics workspace and write a scheduled query rule
In Microsoft Defender for Cloud, enable the Defender CSPM plan so vault behaviour is evaluated by the security graph
cards.answer: In Microsoft Defender for Cloud, open Environment settings, choose the subscription, and toggle the Key Vault plan on
cards.why: Defender for Key Vault is a Defender for Cloud plan enabled per subscription from Environment settings, and once on it produces behavioural alerts without agents or hand-written detections. The closest wrong answer is the vault's Security page: that is where the resulting alerts are displayed, which makes it feel like the enablement point, but the toggle is not there. Diagnostic logging plus a query rule is the do-it-yourself alternative the plan exists to replace, and Defender CSPM handles posture and exposed secrets, not vault access anomalies.
cards.citation: Defender for Key Vault plan · outline 1.2

cards.q: It is 02:40. A Defender for Cloud alert with the identifier KV_ListGetAnomaly is firing on the vault behind a retailer's payment gateway: a service principal belonging to a reporting job has just enumerated every secret and is pulling them one after another. The job's owner is asleep and the reads are still arriving. What do you do first?
options: Cut the principal's access to the vault by removing its role assignment, then rotate every secret the alert lists as read
Add a suppression rule for this alert, because the reporting job is a known internal workload and the noise is masking other signals
Enable purge protection on the vault so the attacker cannot destroy the secrets after copying them
Delete the vault so that soft delete preserves the objects while the investigation runs
cards.answer: Cut the principal's access to the vault by removing its role assignment, then rotate every secret the alert lists as read
cards.why: The documented response is to restrict or remove the suspicious security principal and then immediately rotate every key, secret and certificate the alert shows as accessed, since a recognisable identity is exactly what stolen credentials look like. Suppression is the dangerous near miss: it is a legitimate tool for known noise, but the guidance is explicit that you must not dismiss an alert merely because you recognise the caller. Purge protection guards against destruction rather than exfiltration, and deleting the vault causes an outage while doing nothing about the copied material.
cards.citation: Overview of Microsoft Defender for Key Vault (respond to alerts) · outline 1.2

cards.q: A children's charity gets a KV_SuspiciousIPAccess alert: a vault has been successfully reached from an address flagged by Microsoft threat intelligence, and the address maps to no tenant resource anyone recognises. The vault's firewall has never been turned on, so it accepts requests from anywhere. Containment now, before the deeper investigation. What is the move?
options: Enable the vault firewall and admit only the virtual networks and public addresses the legitimate workloads use
Set the vault's public network access to Secure by perimeter and rely on the trusted Microsoft services bypass for the applications
Disable every key and secret in the vault until the source of the traffic has been identified
Raise the vault to the Premium tier so the key material is protected inside a hardware security module
cards.answer: Enable the vault firewall and admit only the virtual networks and public addresses the legitimate workloads use
cards.why: For traffic from an unrecognised address the documented containment is to switch on the Key Vault firewall and then configure it with the trusted resources and virtual networks, which shuts the door without stopping the business. The plausible-looking alternative is Secure by perimeter, but associating the vault with a perimeter running in enforced mode overrides the trusted services bypass, so first-party dependencies break unless explicit perimeter rules already admit them, which is not a change to make mid-incident. Disabling everything takes the charity's applications down, and the tier has no bearing on who can reach the endpoint.
cards.citation: Defender for Key Vault overview and Key Vault network security configuration · outline 1.2

cards.q: A departing contractor at a manufacturer deleted the vault key that wraps a production storage account, twelve minutes ago. Soft delete is on with the default retention; purge protection was never enabled. Applications are already failing on encrypted reads and the key name cannot be reused while it sits deleted. What restores service?
options: Recover the soft-deleted key in place, which returns it under the same identifier the storage account is configured with
Restore last night's key backup into a standby vault and repoint the storage account at the restored copy
Recreate an identically named key in that same vault so the storage account's reference resolves again
Purge the deleted key and let the storage account fall back to Microsoft-managed keys until a replacement is issued
cards.answer: Recover the soft-deleted key in place, which returns it under the same identifier the storage account is configured with
cards.why: A deleted object stays recoverable throughout the retention window and recovery undoes the deletion in place, so the existing key identifier and the dependent service both come back without reconfiguration. Restoring the backup elsewhere is the closest wrong answer and would eventually work, but it produces a fully independent copy under a different vault and demands that the storage account be repointed, which is slower and riskier while an outage runs. A same-name key cannot be created while the deleted object occupies that name, and purging destroys the material irrecoverably.
cards.citation: Azure Key Vault soft-delete overview (object recovery) · outline 1.2

cards.q: Threat intelligence tells a bank that a vault key used both for SQL transparent data encryption and for a storage account's customer-managed key may have been exposed by a compromised build host. An engineer's hand is hovering over the Disable button on that key. What should happen instead?
options: Rotate to new key material, migrate the SQL databases and the storage account onto it, and only then disable the old key
Disable the key immediately to stop any use of the exposed material, then rebuild the dependent services onto a replacement
Delete the key so soft delete keeps it recoverable while the dependent services are pointed at a new one
Purge every backup copy of the key first, so no restored copy can be used with the exposed material
cards.answer: Rotate to new key material, migrate the SQL databases and the storage account onto it, and only then disable the old key
cards.why: Disabling or deleting a key takes every dependent service offline at once, so transparent data encryption databases become inaccessible and the storage account starts returning errors; the documented compromise response is to rotate and migrate dependants before removing the old key. Disabling first is the instinctive wrong move and converts a suspected exposure into a certain outage. Deleting is that same outage with extra steps, and purging backups neither contains the exposure nor helps the migration, since a restored copy is independent of the original anyway.
cards.citation: Secure your Azure Key Vault (backup copy independence and key compromise response) · outline 1.2

cards.q: The manufacturer from the deletion incident holds its post-incident review. The finding is blunt: one credential was one command away from destroying key material permanently. The team wants a control that makes irreversible destruction impossible for the retention window, and wants it proven across every subscription rather than promised. What goes into the plan?
options: Enable purge protection on the vaults and use Azure Policy to audit and enforce it estate-wide, accepting that it cannot be switched off afterwards
Rely on soft delete, which is already on by default and holds deleted objects for the retention period
Restrict the Key Vault Purge Operator role to a two-person break-glass group and review the membership each quarter
Schedule nightly exports of every key, secret and certificate to a locked storage account in a separate subscription
cards.answer: Enable purge protection on the vaults and use Azure Policy to audit and enforce it estate-wide, accepting that it cannot be switched off afterwards
cards.why: Purge protection is not on by default, requires soft delete, and once enabled it blocks purging of a deleted vault or object until the retention period elapses, which is the only setting that makes destruction genuinely impossible for that window; Azure Policy is the documented way to prove it across an estate. Soft delete alone is the closest wrong answer, and it is exactly what failed to reassure the review, because a privileged caller can still purge inside the window. Constraining the Purge Operator role and taking backups are worthwhile companions but both remain reversible by a sufficiently privileged identity.
cards.citation: Key Vault soft-delete with purge protection, plus vault hardening guidance · outline 1.2

cards.q: A retail bank's quarterly access review shows eleven engineers holding standing Key Vault Administrator on the production vaults, granted years ago for a migration that finished long since. Nobody can name a day in the last quarter when the rights were used. What should the hardening plan put in place?
options: Make the administrator assignments eligible through Privileged Identity Management, requiring approval and multifactor authentication at activation
Move the assignments up to the management group so one review covers every vault and drift between subscriptions stops
Replace the role assignments with a legacy access policy granting the engineers only the key and secret permissions they actually use
Keep the standing assignments and add an alert rule that notifies the security team whenever an administrator reads a secret
cards.answer: Make the administrator assignments eligible through Privileged Identity Management, requiring approval and multifactor authentication at activation
cards.why: The recommended posture is just-in-time privileged access: Privileged Identity Management makes the roles eligible rather than permanent, and requiring an approver plus multifactor authentication at activation removes the always-on blast radius the review found. Reverting to access policies is the trap, because it looks like tightening but the legacy model has known weaknesses and no Privileged Identity Management support, which is one of the reasons Azure RBAC is recommended. Raising the scope to a management group widens the standing grant rather than shrinking it, and alerting only tells you afterwards that the rights were used.
cards.citation: Secure your Azure Key Vault (identity and access management, just-in-time roles) · outline 1.2

cards.q: A car-parts manufacturer has roughly 900 resources already deployed across four production subscriptions, and finance cannot allocate spend because most of them carry no costCenter tag. The platform team wants the tag stamped onto every existing resource, and onto everything created from now on, without asking each application team to redeploy. Which Azure Policy approach delivers that?
options: Assign a definition that uses the modify effect, give the assignment a managed identity with the right role, then run a remediation task over the existing resources
Assign a definition that uses the append effect, then wait for the next compliance evaluation cycle to stamp the existing resources
Assign a definition that uses the deny effect so untagged resources are rejected until each team adds the tag themselves
Assign a definition that uses auditIfNotExists and attach a workflow automation logic app to write the tag when a resource is flagged
cards.answer: Assign a definition that uses the modify effect, give the assignment a managed identity with the right role, then run a remediation task over the existing resources
cards.why: Modify adds, updates or removes properties and tags during create or update, and non-compliant resources that already exist can be brought into line with a remediation task that runs under the assignment identity. The nearest wrong answer is append: it also alters a request, but it only acts on the incoming create or update call and there is no remediation-task path for it, so the 900 existing resources stay untagged forever.
cards.citation: Azure Policy definition structure, modify effect and remediation tasks · outline 1.3

cards.q: A university's central IT group has authored a policy that denies storage accounts allowing public blob access. Forty research subscriptions sit under the management group, and the research computing director has warned that a surprise deny will break grant deadlines. IT wants a full compliance picture for two weeks before anything is actually blocked. How should the assignment be created?
options: Assign it with enforcementMode set to DoNotEnforce, review the compliance results, then switch to Default
Assign it and immediately add an override on the assignment that replaces the effect with disabled for the first two weeks
Assign it and create a policy exemption with the Waiver category on each of the forty subscriptions, with expiresOn set to two weeks out
Assign it with a resourceSelector that matches no resource type, then widen the selector after two weeks
cards.answer: Assign it with enforcementMode set to DoNotEnforce, review the compliance results, then switch to Default
cards.why: DoNotEnforce evaluates the assignment and reports compliance while withholding the effect, and it also keeps deny entries out of the Azure Activity log, which is exactly the dry run being asked for. The closest wrong option is the disabled override: disabled stops the policy producing a compliance result at all, so after two weeks the team would have learned nothing about how many storage accounts would have been blocked.
cards.citation: Azure Policy assignment structure, enforcementMode and overrides · outline 1.3

cards.q: A retail bank is preparing for a card-scheme assessment. Its twenty-four Azure subscriptions all sit under one management group, and the assessor wants a single continuously assessed view of payment-card control coverage rather than twenty-four separate reports. Defender for Cloud is already onboarded with the Defender CSPM plan. What should the security administrator do?
options: In Defender for Cloud Regulatory compliance, open Manage compliance policies, select the management group, and turn on the PCI DSS v4.0.1 standard
Turn on the MCSB v2 preview benchmark on each subscription, since it carries the expanded regulatory control mappings
Build a custom standard containing KQL custom recommendations that reproduce the payment-card control set
Raise a Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager assessment for payment-card controls and export its score as the evidence
cards.answer: In Defender for Cloud Regulatory compliance, open Manage compliance policies, select the management group, and turn on the PCI DSS v4.0.1 standard
cards.why: Regulatory standards in Defender for Cloud are delivered as Azure Policy initiatives that you assign to a scope, and Microsoft's guidance is to pick the highest applicable scope so compliance data aggregates across every nested subscription. The nearest wrong option is MCSB v2: it is a benchmark of Microsoft's own cloud security principles with broader policy mappings, not the card-scheme standard, so it will never produce the control-by-control evidence the assessor asked for.
cards.citation: Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance standards and Assign regulatory compliance standards · outline 1.3

cards.q: A hospital group's internal standard says every Kubernetes cluster hosting clinical workloads must carry a dataClassification tag and sit in an approved region pair. No built-in Defender for Cloud recommendation checks that pairing, but the CISO wants the gap to appear on the same dashboard as everything else and to count toward posture. Defender CSPM is licensed. What is the right build?
options: Author a custom recommendation using Kusto Query Language inside a custom standard, so it surfaces alongside the built-in recommendations
Author a custom Azure Policy definition and add it to the Microsoft cloud security benchmark standard so it inherits benchmark reporting
Create a governance rule that assigns an owner and a due date for clusters missing the tag
Create an exemption on the existing Kubernetes recommendations and track the rule in a separate workbook
cards.answer: Author a custom recommendation using Kusto Query Language inside a custom standard, so it surfaces alongside the built-in recommendations
cards.why: Custom recommendations let you define your own assessment logic in KQL, they are created within a custom standard, and once created they appear with the built-in recommendations and contribute to the posture assessment. The nearest wrong option is bolting a custom definition onto MCSB: MCSB is a built-in benchmark whose control set you do not extend, so a custom check has to live in a custom standard, not inside the benchmark.
cards.citation: Defender for Cloud security policies, custom standards and custom recommendations · outline 1.3

cards.q: A logistics firm keeps failing the MCSB recommendation that storage accounts restrict network reach through virtual network rules, because developers create wide-open accounts faster than the platform team can fix them. The security lead's requirement is blunt: a storage account that does not meet the criteria must not come into existence at all. In Defender for Cloud, which action on that recommendation meets it?
options: Select Deny on the recommendation so non-compliant storage accounts are blocked at creation
Select Enforce on the recommendation so Defender for Cloud remediates it automatically at creation
Assign a governance rule with a short SLA so the recommendation becomes overdue quickly and pushes the owner to act
Use Manage effect and parameters to set the recommendation to Disabled and rely on a separate custom standard
cards.answer: Select Deny on the recommendation so non-compliant storage accounts are blocked at creation
cards.why: Deny prevents deployment of resources that do not comply with the benchmark control, which is the only option that stops the resource existing. The nearest wrong option is Enforce: it uses the DeployIfNotExists effect to automatically remediate non-compliant resources after they are created, so the wide-open account still gets created and only then gets fixed. Both actions apply to Azure recommendations and only to a subset of them.
cards.citation: Manage MCSB recommendations in Defender for Cloud, deny and enforce · outline 1.3

cards.q: A payments company keeps its HSM-backed key vault in a production resource group. After a near-miss where a subscription Owner nearly deleted it during a cleanup, the platform lead wants deletion of that one vault blocked for everybody regardless of their role, while the network team must still be able to edit the vault firewall rules daily. What should be applied?
options: A Delete lock, called CanNotDelete on the command line, on the key vault resource
A Read-only lock, called ReadOnly on the command line, on the key vault resource
A deployment stack over the resource group with the deny settings mode set to deny write and delete
Removal of all Owner assignments on the subscription, replaced by eligible Owner assignments in Privileged Identity Management
cards.answer: A Delete lock, called CanNotDelete on the command line, on the key vault resource
cards.why: A CanNotDelete lock lets authorized users read and modify the resource but not delete it, and unlike RBAC a management lock applies across all users and roles, which is the do-not-trust-the-Owner requirement here. The nearest wrong option is the ReadOnly lock: it blocks updates as well as deletion, so the network team could no longer change the vault firewall, and it behaves roughly like restricting everyone to Reader.
cards.citation: Azure resource locks guidance · outline 1.3

cards.q: A media company wants its service-desk team to onboard new starters by granting them two specific job-function roles at subscription scope, and nothing else. Handing the service desk the ability to grant any role, including Owner, is exactly what the last audit finding was about. Which assignment fits?
options: Assign Role Based Access Control Administrator to the service-desk group and add a condition that constrains which roles they may assign
Assign User Access Administrator to the service-desk group at subscription scope
Assign Owner to the service-desk group at each resource group instead of the subscription
Create a custom role whose Actions include a wildcard over the authorization resource provider and assign it at subscription scope
cards.answer: Assign Role Based Access Control Administrator to the service-desk group and add a condition that constrains which roles they may assign
cards.why: Where you assign a role that carries permission to create role assignments, Microsoft's guidance is to add a condition that constrains the delegation, and that is what turns unbounded role granting into two named roles. The nearest wrong option is User Access Administrator: it is a privileged administrator role, and unconditioned it lets the service desk grant anything at all, which recreates the audit finding. Assigning to the group rather than to individuals is also the recommended pattern.
cards.citation: Best practices for Azure RBAC, delegate role assignment management with conditions · outline 1.3

cards.q: A software house brings in a contractor for six months to look after app registrations for one product. The contractor needs directory permissions over that single application object and must not gain any permission over Azure subscriptions or resource groups. Which build satisfies this?
options: Create a Microsoft Entra custom role from the preset permission list and assign it at the app registration object scope, licensing the contractor with Entra ID P1
Create an Azure custom role and set its AssignableScopes to the tenant root scope so it covers directory objects as well
Create an Azure custom role containing DataActions and assign it at management group scope so it spans the whole estate
Add the contractor to a role-assignable group that holds Contributor at subscription scope and set an expiry on the membership
cards.answer: Create a Microsoft Entra custom role from the preset permission list and assign it at the app registration object scope, licensing the contractor with Entra ID P1
cards.why: Entra custom roles are built from a preset permission list and can be assigned at the directory scope or at an app registration resource scope, and each user holding a custom role assignment needs an Entra ID P1 license. The nearest wrong option is the Azure custom role at root: Azure RBAC governs Azure resources rather than directory objects, and in any case AssignableScopes cannot be set to the root scope. The DataActions option fails too, because a custom role with DataActions cannot be assigned at management group scope.
cards.citation: Azure custom roles and Microsoft Entra ID RBAC overview · outline 1.3

cards.q: An insurer's access audit finds fourteen service principals holding Owner at subscription scope, all assigned more than ninety days ago, each one belonging to a deployment pipeline that only ever touches a single resource group. The security architect must cut this exposure without stopping the pipelines. What should be done?
options: Replace each Owner assignment with a narrower job function role scoped to the resource group that the pipeline actually deploys into
Convert each Owner assignment into an eligible assignment in Privileged Identity Management so the pipeline must activate before deploying
Leave the assignments in place and apply a Delete lock to each subscription so the service principals cannot destroy anything
Leave the assignments in place and set up a Microsoft Entra access review of the Global Administrator role
cards.answer: Replace each Owner assignment with a narrower job function role scoped to the resource group that the pipeline actually deploys into
cards.why: The guidance is to avoid a privileged administrator role where a job function role will do, and where a privileged role is unavoidable to use a narrow scope such as a resource group rather than a subscription. The nearest wrong option is the PIM conversion, and it is wrong on a hard mechanical point: an eligible role assignment can be created for a user but never for an application, a service principal or a managed identity, since a non-human principal has no way to run the activation step.
cards.citation: Azure RBAC best practices and time-bound eligible assignments · outline 1.3

cards.q: A grocery chain ships its landing zone as Bicep from a pipeline. Application teams hold Contributor on the workload resource groups and keep hand-editing the shared firewall and route tables, which then drift back on the next release. The platform lead wants those pipeline-managed resources blocked from any out-of-band write or delete, with the pipeline identity itself still able to change them. What should be deployed?
options: A deployment stack held at the parent subscription scope, with deny settings mode set to deny write and delete and the pipeline principal listed in the excluded principals
Read-only locks on each pipeline-managed resource, removed and reapplied by the pipeline on every release
An Azure Policy assignment with a deny effect on the deployment resource type so only the pipeline can submit deployments
A template spec published to a locked resource group, with Contributor removed from the application teams
cards.answer: A deployment stack held at the parent subscription scope, with deny settings mode set to deny write and delete and the pipeline principal listed in the excluded principals
cards.why: A deployment stack creates a deny assignment over the resources it manages, the deny settings mode chooses between none, deny delete and deny write and delete, and up to five Entra principal IDs can be excluded from the lock so the pipeline keeps working. Holding the stack at the parent scope keeps the teams from editing the stack itself. The nearest wrong option is the read-only locks: locks can be removed by anyone holding the authorization lock actions, and a pipeline that strips its own locks each release protects nothing between runs.
cards.citation: Bicep deployment stacks with managed-resource protection · outline 1.3

cards.q: It is 03:20. A hospital trust's on-call engineer is watching an attacker, using stolen backup admin credentials, walk through the Recovery Services vault running Stop backup with Delete backup data against forty clinical VMs. Credentials have just been revoked. The backup items now show in red with no recovery points and a countdown. What is the containment move for the data?
options: Undelete each soft deleted backup item from the vault, then explicitly select Resume backup, because undelete leaves the item in a stop-with-retain-data state
Undelete each soft deleted backup item and confirm the schedule, since scheduled backups restart automatically once the item is recovered
Disable soft delete on the vault so the items leave the soft deleted state and the original schedule takes over
Fail the clinical VMs over to the geo-secondary region, since deleted backup data cannot be recovered from the primary vault
cards.answer: Undelete each soft deleted backup item from the vault, then explicitly select Resume backup, because undelete leaves the item in a stop-with-retain-data state
cards.why: Soft delete is on by default and holds deleted backup data for a retention window before permanent deletion, and the portal offers Undelete on the red items. The nearest wrong option is the one that assumes backups resume by themselves: undeleting reinstates the item into stop-backup-with-retain-data and does not restart the schedule, so without an explicit Resume backup the trust recovers its old recovery points but takes no new ones. Disabling soft delete would move in exactly the wrong direction.
cards.citation: Soft delete in Azure Backup, configuration and management · outline 1.3

cards.q: Ransomware is spreading through a steelmaker's plant network right now. The intruder has the backup admin account and is repeatedly attempting to disable soft delete on the Recovery Services vault and cut retention on the policies. Every attempt is failing authorization. The vault is associated with a Resource Guard owned by the security team, and the backup admin was granted the Backup MUA Operator role on it last week for a migration. What does the security admin do in the next five minutes?
options: Remove the backup admin's Backup MUA Operator role assignment on the Resource Guard so the protected critical operations keep failing
Remove the backup admin's Contributor role on the Recovery Services vault, which is what multi-user authorization actually checks
Enable immutability on the vault now, which will retroactively block the operations already attempted
Apply a CannotDelete lock to the Azure Backup-created resource group for the vault so nothing inside it can be removed
cards.answer: Remove the backup admin's Backup MUA Operator role assignment on the Resource Guard so the protected critical operations keep failing
cards.why: Multi-user authorization works by requiring permission on a separate Resource Guard resource, and disabling soft delete and removing MUA protection are mandatory protected operations that cannot be excluded. Pulling the temporarily granted Backup MUA Operator role is the switch that keeps the attempts failing. The nearest wrong option is removing Contributor on the vault: MUA evaluates permissions on the Resource Guard, not on the vault, so vault-side role changes do not close this path. The lock option is actively harmful, because a cannot-delete lock on the Backup-created resource group makes backups fail once restore points cannot be cleaned up.
cards.citation: Multiuser authorization using Resource Guard and Lock your Azure resources · outline 1.3

cards.q: Black Friday, 11:00. A retailer's checkout tier needs to scale out and two stuck VMs need restarting, but every attempt fails. Twenty minutes ago a governance engineer applied a Read-only lock at the resource group holding the App Service plan and the VMs. The subscription Owner has already tried and also cannot start the VMs. What restores service?
options: Replace the Read-only lock on that resource group with a Delete lock, since a read-only lock blocks the POST operations that start a VM or scale a plan
Grant the on-call team Owner on the resource group, since a lock only restricts principals below Owner
Add resource-level locks set to Delete on the individual VMs, since the most specific lock in the chain wins over the parent
Move the VMs to an unlocked resource group, then start them there
cards.answer: Replace the Read-only lock on that resource group with a Delete lock, since a read-only lock blocks the POST operations that start a VM or scale a plan
cards.why: Starting or restarting a VM and scaling an App Service plan are POST operations, and a read-only lock on the containing resource group blocks them for all users, while a cannot-delete lock still allows read and modify. The nearest wrong option is granting Owner: management locks apply across all users and roles and override permissions, so no role assignment gets past them. Adding a child lock does not help either, because an inherited parent lock still wins wherever it is the stricter of the two, and a read-only lock at resource group level also stops you relocating existing resources out of that group.
cards.citation: Azure resource locks, inheritance and considerations · outline 1.3

cards.q: A bank is mid-incident and the forensics team has found that four key vaults created in the last fortnight have no diagnostic settings, so there are no logs of the attacker's access. A deployIfNotExists assignment was supposed to deploy those settings. Its compliance results show the vaults as non-compliant, and running a remediation task returns an authorization failure. What is the fix that gets logging onto the remaining vaults now?
options: Re-grant the assignment's managed identity the role it needs at the assignment scope, then re-run the remediation task with the ReEvaluateCompliance discovery setting
Set the assignment's enforcementMode to Default, because remediation tasks cannot run while the assignment is set to DoNotEnforce
Change the definition's effect from deployIfNotExists to deny so that vaults without diagnostic settings can no longer be created
Recreate the assignment with a system-assigned managed identity and set its location property to global so it can remediate in every region
cards.answer: Re-grant the assignment's managed identity the role it needs at the assignment scope, then re-run the remediation task with the ReEvaluateCompliance discovery setting
cards.why: A deployIfNotExists assignment always deploys under the assignment identity, so an authorization failure on the remediation task points straight at that identity's missing role, and re-discovery with ReEvaluateCompliance forces a fresh scan before remediating. Granting the identity its permissions needs User Access Administrator. The nearest wrong option is the enforcementMode change: remediation tasks for deployIfNotExists policies can be started even when enforcementMode is DoNotEnforce, so that would burn time and fix nothing. The last option is invalid outright, since an assignment identity's location cannot be global.
cards.citation: Azure Policy assignment structure identity, remediation tasks and resource discovery mode · outline 1.3

cards.q: After the incident, an insurer's governance board asks why fourteen standing Owner assignments had been sitting unreviewed for months. The security architect is asked for a durable control, not another spreadsheet, that keeps subscription-level privilege from silently accumulating again. What should be put in place?
options: Schedule recurring Azure resource access reviews over the privileged assignments, and move human administrators to time-bound or eligible assignments in Privileged Identity Management
Track the role assignment count chart for each subscription and act whenever it approaches the four thousand assignment limit
Watch the Defender for Cloud secure score and treat any drop as the trigger to re-examine role assignments
Replace the built-in privileged roles with a single custom role that uses a wildcard action, so all privilege sits in one definition that is easy to inspect
cards.answer: Schedule recurring Azure resource access reviews over the privileged assignments, and move human administrators to time-bound or eligible assignments in Privileged Identity Management
cards.why: PIM lowers the exposure time of privilege by making access just-in-time and time-bound so it is revoked automatically, and access reviews over Azure resources, which require Owner or User Access Administrator to create, give the recurring attestation the board is asking for. The nearest wrong option is the assignment-count chart: the four thousand per-subscription limit is a capacity guardrail and says nothing about whether any given assignment is still justified. The wildcard custom role is the opposite of the guidance, which is to specify actions explicitly.
cards.citation: Best practices for Azure RBAC, PIM integration and listing role assignments · outline 1.3

cards.q: A pharmaceutical manufacturer has just spent a week untangling a governance outage caused by a policy someone authored directly in the portal against one subscription, which then blocked a validated manufacturing deployment. The platform team is rebuilding how policy reaches the estate. Which target-state pipeline should they adopt?
