options: Hold definitions in source control, deploy them to a management group as the definition location, assign them in DoNotEnforce first, then flip to Default and enable remediation tasks
Hold definitions in source control but keep the definition location at each subscription, so a bad definition can only ever affect one subscription
Keep authoring in the portal but wrap every assignment in an exemption with the Mitigated category that the change board removes after review
Replace policy definitions with deployment stacks configured for detach on unmanage, so governance and deployment share one artifact
cards.answer: Hold definitions in source control, deploy them to a management group as the definition location, assign them in DoNotEnforce first, then flip to Default and enable remediation tasks
cards.why: Policy as code puts exported definitions under source control, validates the updated definition before it is enforced, then moves to enforced assignments and enables remediation tasks, and a definition has to be located at either a subscription or a management group, and only the management group choice gives the assignable reach a whole estate needs. The nearest wrong option is pinning the definition location to each subscription: it does limit blast radius, but a definition can only be assigned within the hierarchy of its definition location, so the team would be maintaining duplicate definitions per subscription, which is the sprawl that caused the outage. Deployment stacks protect deployed resources, they do not evaluate compliance.
cards.citation: Design Azure Policy as Code workflows and Azure Policy definition structure, definition location · outline 1.3

cards.q: A retail bank runs a payments reconciliation job that reads blobs using an account SAS embedded in its config. Security wants the storage account to reject every request that is authorised with the account access keys, and has scheduled the change for Sunday night. What will happen to the reconciliation job once Allow storage account key access is set to Disabled?
options: The job breaks, because an account SAS carries a signature made from the account key, so it is denied across all storage services once Shared Key is disallowed
The job continues, because a SAS is a separate authorisation type and is unaffected by the Shared Key setting
The job continues until the SAS reaches its stated expiry time, after which it cannot be renewed
The job breaks only for blob endpoints, because the restriction applies to Blob Storage and leaves queue, table and file endpoints working
cards.answer: The job breaks, because an account SAS carries a signature made from the account key, so it is denied across all storage services once Shared Key is disallowed
cards.why: Both the account SAS and the service SAS take their signature from the storage account key, so Azure Storage denies them for every service once AllowSharedKeyAccess is false; only a user delegation SAS, signed with Microsoft Entra credentials, keeps working. The nearest wrong answer is the one that treats SAS as its own authorisation type: the metrics blade lumps all SAS together, but the underlying signing key is what decides, and only Entra-signed tokens survive. Nothing about the change waits for an existing token to expire.
cards.citation: Azure Storage: disabling Shared Key authorization · outline 2.1

cards.q: A university research office hands a partner lab a service SAS for one blob container. Legal insists that if the partnership ends mid-term, access must be cut off the same afternoon without regenerating the storage account keys that a dozen other systems depend on. How should the SAS be issued?
options: Bind the service SAS to a stored access policy on the container, so the policy can be deleted or its expiry moved into the past
Issue an ad hoc service SAS with a signed IP field naming the partner's public address range
Issue an account SAS scoped to the Blob service and rely on the SAS expiration policy configured on the account
Grant the partner the Storage Blob Data Reader role on the container and remove the role assignment when the partnership ends
cards.answer: Bind the service SAS to a stored access policy on the container, so the policy can be deleted or its expiry moved into the past
cards.why: A stored access policy is defined on the container and supplies the start time, expiry and permissions to any service SAS that references it, so deleting the policy, renaming it, or pushing its expiry into the past revokes every SAS bound to it without touching the account keys. The closest wrong option, an ad hoc SAS with a signed IP range, narrows who can use the token but gives you no revocation lever short of key regeneration. The RBAC option is sound practice generally but the requirement was explicitly to deliver a SAS.
cards.citation: Azure Storage: shared access signature (SAS) delegated access · outline 2.1

cards.q: A grocery chain's platform engineer adds the app subnet as a virtual network rule on the storage account holding price files, saves, and then finds that a laptop on the office network can still download blobs over the public endpoint. Nothing was blocked. What did the engineer miss?
options: The network rule set default action is still Allow, so rules have no effect until it is set to Deny
The subnet needs the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint enabled before any rule takes effect
The account needs a private endpoint, because virtual network rules only apply to accounts reachable over Private Link
The Allow Azure services on the trusted services list exception is switched on and is admitting the office traffic
cards.answer: The network rule set default action is still Allow, so rules have no effect until it is set to Deny
cards.why: Network rules do nothing while the default action remains Allow: the portal switch or the Deny value on default-action is what closes the public endpoint, and only then do the allow-list entries matter. The nearest wrong answer, the missing service endpoint, is a real requirement for the subnet to reach the account privately, and the portal creates it for you when you pick the subnet, but it would never have explained office traffic still getting through. The trusted services exception admits named Azure services, not an employee laptop.
cards.citation: Azure Storage virtual network rules · outline 2.1

cards.q: A car parts manufacturer runs its ERP subnet in West Europe but the telemetry storage account it must reach sits in North Europe. The subnet already has the Azure Storage service endpoint enabled and the storage firewall lists the subnet, yet requests to the North Europe account are refused. Which change fixes it?
options: Replace the subnet's Microsoft.Storage service endpoint with the Microsoft.Storage.Global cross-region service endpoint
Add the subnet's outbound NAT public IP address as an IP network rule on the storage account
Add both the Microsoft.Storage and Microsoft.Storage.Global service endpoints to the subnet
Peer the two virtual networks and add a resource instance rule for the ERP application
cards.answer: Replace the subnet's Microsoft.Storage service endpoint with the Microsoft.Storage.Global cross-region service endpoint
cards.why: The plain Microsoft.Storage endpoint only reaches accounts sitting in whichever region hosts the virtual network; Microsoft.Storage.Global reaches accounts in any region, and a subnet can carry only one of the two, so the existing endpoint must be removed first. The nearest wrong option, adding an IP rule, fails because once a service endpoint is enabled the traffic leaves with a private source address and IP rules for that subnet stop having any effect. Resource instance rules are for Azure services that cannot be isolated by subnet or IP at all.
cards.citation: Azure Storage firewall and network access rules · outline 2.1

cards.q: A hospital trust must encrypt its imaging archive with keys the trust controls. The storage admin creates a new key vault, generates an RSA 2048 key, grants the storage account's managed identity wrap, unwrap and get, then tries to point the storage account at the key. The portal refuses the vault. What is missing on the vault?
options: Both soft delete and purge protection must be enabled on the key vault
The vault must be converted to a Managed HSM, because software-protected keys cannot wrap a storage account key
The vault must reside in the storage account's own subscription and region
The key must be RSA 4096, because 2048-bit keys are not accepted for storage account encryption
cards.answer: Both soft delete and purge protection must be enabled on the key vault
cards.why: A key vault or managed HSM holding a customer-managed key for Azure Storage must have soft delete and purge protection turned on, so an accidental key deletion cannot orphan the data permanently. The nearest wrong option, forcing a Managed HSM, confuses an assurance choice with a requirement, since a standard vault is fully supported and the two share the same configuration APIs. Region, subscription and tenant may all differ from the storage account, and RSA 2048, 3072 and 4096 are all accepted.
cards.citation: Customer-managed keys for Azure Storage encryption · outline 2.1

cards.q: A defence subcontractor's assurance team wants storage data encrypted twice, with two different algorithms and two different keys, so that compromise of one key or cipher still leaves the data protected. The platform team already runs customer-managed keys on the existing accounts. What should they tell the assurance team?
options: Enable infrastructure encryption, which must be chosen when the storage account is created and adds a second Microsoft-managed key layer
Enable infrastructure encryption on the existing accounts from the Encryption blade, choosing a second customer-managed key
Add a second customer-managed key as an encryption scope on each container, which layers over the account key
Turn on client-side encryption version 2 in the application, which is what the platform means by double encryption
cards.answer: Enable infrastructure encryption, which must be chosen when the storage account is created and adds a second Microsoft-managed key layer
cards.why: Infrastructure encryption adds a second 256-bit AES layer beneath service-side encryption, always using a separate Microsoft-managed key, and it is a create-time property of the storage account rather than something you switch on afterwards. The nearest wrong option gets the feature right but both the timing and the key ownership wrong: the infrastructure layer never uses your customer-managed key. Encryption scopes change the scope of the service-level key, they do not stack a second layer, and client-side encryption is an application-side control the assurance team did not ask for.
cards.citation: Azure Storage encryption for data at rest · outline 2.1

cards.q: A logistics operator locks a storage account down to two subnets with a Deny default action. The next morning the SOC notices that diagnostic logs from the fleet-tracking Azure SQL servers have stopped landing in that account, and Azure Monitor can no longer write resource logs either. Which configuration restores the flow without opening the account to the internet?
options: Add a network security exception for trusted Azure services, which covers Microsoft.Insights and Microsoft.Sql writing to the account
Add IP network rules covering the published outbound address ranges of Azure Monitor and Azure SQL in that region
Add the Log Analytics workspace subnet as a virtual network rule with the storage service endpoint enabled
Switch the account's network routing preference to Microsoft global network routing
cards.answer: Add a network security exception for trusted Azure services, which covers Microsoft.Insights and Microsoft.Sql writing to the account
cards.why: Azure Monitor and Azure SQL both operate outside any subnet you control, so the supported route is the trusted Azure services exception, which lets those resource providers reach the account using strong authentication while the firewall stays closed to everything else. The nearest wrong option, chasing service IP ranges, is unmaintainable and is not how these services are admitted. A Log Analytics workspace is not a subnet you can add a rule for, and routing preference changes the path traffic takes, not who is authorised to arrive.
cards.citation: Azure Storage network security: trusted services exception · outline 2.1

cards.q: A media company enables Defender for Storage with malware scanning on the account that receives partner video uploads. Three weeks into the month, the SOC gets an alert saying scanning has stopped for that account, and new uploads are landing unscanned. Nothing was disabled. What most likely happened?
options: The account hit its monthly on-upload scanning cap, which defaults to 10,000 GB of uploaded blob data per account each month
The uploads exceeded the 50 GB per-blob size limit, so the scanner skipped them and paused the plan
The Defender for Storage plan reverted to the classic plan, which does not include malware scanning
Hash reputation analysis replaced full scanning because the uploads arrived through Put Block and Put Block List
cards.answer: The account hit its monthly on-upload scanning cap, which defaults to 10,000 GB of uploaded blob data per account each month
cards.why: Malware scanning is billed per gigabyte scanned and carries a per-account monthly cap that defaults to 10,000 GB of uploaded blobs, with an alert at 75 percent and a second alert when scanning pauses for the rest of the month. The nearest wrong option, the 50 GB blob size limit, is real but produces a Not Scanned result for that single oversized blob with a SAM error code, not a halt across the account. The classic plan does not spontaneously return, and hash reputation analysis is a separate capability rather than a fallback the service switches into.
cards.citation: What is Microsoft Defender for Storage · outline 2.1

cards.q: A city council's identity team wants Conditional Access to apply to the storage account holding planning case files, so that data access requires a compliant device. They have already assigned Storage Blob Data Reader to the caseworker group. What else is required before Conditional Access can govern access to that account?
options: Shared Key authorization must be disallowed on the storage account
A stored access policy must be created on each container to carry the Conditional Access reference
The account must require secure transfer and a minimum TLS version of 1.2
Anonymous read access must be disabled at the container level
cards.answer: Shared Key authorization must be disallowed on the storage account
cards.why: Conditional Access policies only bite on requests carried by Microsoft Entra identities, so the account must stop accepting key-based authorisation before those policies can protect it; that means setting AllowSharedKeyAccess to false. The nearest wrong option, secure transfer and a TLS floor, is genuinely recommended hardening but neither of those settings has anything to do with which authorisation path a request takes. Disabling anonymous access closes a different hole entirely, and stored access policies belong to service SAS revocation.
cards.citation: Azure Storage: disabling Shared Key authorization · outline 2.1

cards.q: A payroll bureau keeps one container per client company in a single storage account. Two clients now demand that their own data be encrypted under a key only they can have revoked, while the rest of the account stays on the default account key. Redesigning into separate accounts is off the table this quarter. What should the storage architect configure?
options: Encryption scopes on those two containers, each bound to that client's customer-managed key in Key Vault
Customer-managed keys at the account level, rotating the key whenever either client requests revocation
Customer-provided keys supplied by each client on every read and write request to their container
A separate user-assigned managed identity per container, each granted wrap and unwrap on that client's key
cards.answer: Encryption scopes on those two containers, each bound to that client's customer-managed key in Key Vault
cards.why: By default the account encryption key covers the whole account, and encryption scopes exist precisely to draw a key boundary at container or blob level so data belonging to different customers in one account is protected under different keys, backed by Microsoft-managed or customer-managed keys. The nearest wrong option, account-level customer-managed keys, gives one key for everyone, so either client revoking would take down the whole bureau. Customer-provided keys push key handling into every request from the client application, which is not what a per-container boundary requires, and a managed identity is an authorisation principal, not an encryption boundary.
cards.citation: Azure Storage encryption for data at rest · outline 2.1

cards.q: Right now: an insurer's SOC is watching 40 GB an hour of claim documents leave a blob container. The requests carry a valid ad hoc service SAS, three months of validity left, signed with the account key, leaked from a contractor's laptop. It is not bound to any stored access policy. What stops it fastest?
options: Regenerate the storage account key that signed the SAS, invalidating every token signed with it
Create a stored access policy on the container with an expiry in the past so the running SAS inherits it
Set the network firewall default action to Deny and allow only the corporate address range
Remove all Storage Blob Data Contributor role assignments on the container
cards.answer: Regenerate the storage account key that signed the SAS, invalidating every token signed with it
cards.why: An ad hoc service SAS carries its own start time, expiry and permissions in the token and is not revocable on its own, so the only lever that kills it immediately is regenerating the account key that signed it, accepting the collateral breakage of anything else using that key. The nearest wrong option is the stored access policy: a policy only governs tokens that were issued with a reference to it, and creating one after the fact does not retrofit constraints onto a live ad hoc token. Firewall rules may slow the exfiltration if you know the source, but the token stays valid from anywhere you have not blocked, and RBAC assignments never governed this SAS at all.
cards.citation: Azure Storage: shared access signature (SAS) delegated access · outline 2.1

cards.q: Right now: a hospital's document intake account has fired a Defender for Storage alert for a malicious file uploaded to the referrals container. The built-in remediation soft deleted that blob, but the ingestion function reads and forwards every new blob within seconds of upload, well before scan results arrive. What containment move stops clinicians receiving the next one?
options: Apply a Microsoft Entra ABAC condition on the ingestion identity's role assignment so it can only read blobs whose scan result index tag is clean
Raise the blob soft delete retention period on the account from seven days to the maximum
Switch malware scanning from on-upload to on-demand so results exist before the function runs
Add the ingestion function's subnet to the storage firewall and set the default action to Deny
cards.answer: Apply a Microsoft Entra ABAC condition on the ingestion identity's role assignment so it can only read blobs whose scan result index tag is clean
cards.why: Scanning runs in near real time but not instantly, so the gap between upload and result has to be closed on the read side; an ABAC condition keyed to the scan result index tag makes unscanned and malicious blobs unreadable to the consuming application. The nearest wrong option, extending soft delete retention, helps forensics on blobs already caught but does nothing about the race the function is winning. On-demand scanning does not run at upload at all, so it widens the gap, and a firewall rule controls where callers come from, not what they are allowed to read.
cards.citation: Set up automated remediation for malware detection · outline 2.1

cards.q: Right now: a manufacturer's MES has gone read-error across the board. Every blob read on the customer-managed-key storage account returns 403, uploads fail too, and account listing still works. A vault admin was rotating keys twenty minutes ago and disabled the old key version. What is the containment move?
options: Re-enable the disabled key version in the key vault to restore the wrap and unwrap operations
Switch the storage account from customer-managed keys back to Microsoft-managed keys so reads resume
Assign the storage account's managed identity the Key Vault Crypto Officer role so it can select the new version
Restore the affected containers from soft delete, because a 403 on read means the blobs were removed
cards.answer: Re-enable the disabled key version in the key vault to restore the wrap and unwrap operations
cards.why: Disabling the key in the vault is exactly how you revoke a storage account, and the symptom is textbook: data operations that need the account encryption key unwrapped fail with 403 for all users while the account object itself stays visible. Restoring access means restoring the key. The nearest wrong option, flipping back to Microsoft-managed keys, treats a revocation as a configuration preference and does not conjure back the wrapped account key while the vault key is unavailable; the correct sequence is to restore the key first. The storage identity needs wrapkey, unwrapkey and get rather than a broader crypto administration role, and nothing was deleted, so soft delete is irrelevant.
cards.citation: Customer-managed keys for Azure Storage encryption · outline 2.1

cards.q: Right now: an online retailer's SOC has confirmed that a phished engineer's account holds Storage Account Contributor on the order-archive subscription, and the attacker is calling list keys and reading blobs directly with the returned account key. The engineer's session has already been revoked, but the key is now in the attacker's hands. Which move cuts the attacker's data access most decisively?
options: Disable the Allow storage account key access setting on the affected accounts, so all key-signed requests are refused
Regenerate both account keys on the affected accounts
Remove the Storage Account Contributor assignment from the compromised principal
Enable Defender for Storage malware scanning and sensitive data threat detection on the accounts
cards.answer: Disable the Allow storage account key access setting on the affected accounts, so all key-signed requests are refused
cards.why: Disallowing Shared Key makes the storage service reject every request authorised with the account keys, so the stolen key becomes worthless whatever the attacker does next, and only Microsoft Entra requests get through. The nearest wrong option, regenerating the keys, is the reflex answer but it only helps if the attacker has lost the ability to list keys again, and here they still hold a role carrying the list keys action. Removing the role assignment is the right follow-up but does not invalidate a key already exfiltrated, and turning on Defender improves detection rather than stopping the reads in flight.
cards.citation: Azure Storage: disabling Shared Key authorization · outline 2.1

cards.q: After a leaked SAS incident, a university's storage governance review finds several teams still hand-issuing long-lived tokens. The team wants a control that warns issuers and leaves a trace when someone creates a SAS whose validity runs far beyond what the institution considers acceptable. What should they put in place on each account?
options: A SAS expiration policy on the storage account, which warns on over-long service and account SAS and writes an entry to the storage logs
An Azure Policy assignment in Deny mode that blocks creation of SAS tokens longer than the agreed interval
A diagnostic setting that logs SAS generation events to a Log Analytics workspace for weekly review
A stored access policy on every container with the agreed expiry, which all new SAS tokens inherit automatically
cards.answer: A SAS expiration policy on the storage account, which warns on over-long service and account SAS and writes an entry to the storage logs
cards.why: A SAS expiration policy sets a recommended upper bound for service and account SAS; exceeding it surfaces a warning to the issuer and, with Azure Monitor logging enabled, records an entry, which is exactly the warn-and-trace behaviour wanted. The nearest wrong option, an Azure Policy in Deny mode, sounds stronger but SAS tokens are generated client side and are not resource operations that Azure Policy can intercept. Generation of a SAS cannot be audited at all, so a diagnostic setting will not capture it, and stored access policies are inherited only by tokens deliberately issued against them.
cards.citation: Azure Storage: shared access signature (SAS) delegated access · outline 2.1

cards.q: A national bakery chain wants to disallow Shared Key across 300 storage accounts but its last attempt broke a nightly ETL job and was rolled back at 3am. The security lead asks for the sequence that should have been followed before flipping any account. Which approach gets them there safely?
options: Assign the built-in policy for preventing shared key access in audit mode, then use storage metrics filtered on Account Key and SAS plus Log Analytics queries on AuthenticationType to find the calling clients before disallowing
Regenerate the account keys on a pilot group and see which applications raise incidents, then migrate those applications and disallow Shared Key everywhere
Assign the built-in policy in Deny mode across the subscription and let the compliance report list the accounts that fail, then remediate them one at a time
Enable Defender for Storage on all accounts and use its activity monitoring alerts to identify which clients authorise with the account key
cards.answer: Assign the built-in policy for preventing shared key access in audit mode, then use storage metrics filtered on Account Key and SAS plus Log Analytics queries on AuthenticationType to find the calling clients before disallowing
cards.why: The documented sequence is detect, then remediate, then audit and govern: audit mode inventories which accounts still permit Shared Key, the Transactions metric filtered by authentication tells you how much key and SAS traffic there is, and resource logs queried on AuthenticationType name the caller IPs and user agents you must migrate first. The nearest wrong option flips the policy straight to Deny, which stops anyone allowing Shared Key on new accounts but tells you nothing about which applications will break, so it repeats the 3am rollback. Regenerating keys as a discovery technique deliberately causes the outage you are trying to avoid, and Defender for Storage raises alerts on suspicious behaviour rather than producing a per-client authorisation inventory.
cards.citation: Azure Storage: disabling Shared Key authorization · outline 2.1

cards.q: A grocery chain runs forty tenant databases on one logical server in Azure SQL Database. Each tenant's analytics team connects from its own office range, and the chain has been told that a tenant must never be able to reach another tenant's database even if its IP is allowed. The platform team currently maintains one long list of allowed ranges on the server. What should they move to, and how is it configured?
options: Database-level IP firewall rules, created per database with sp_set_database_firewall_rule after the first server-level rule exists
Server-level IP firewall rules narrowed per tenant in the Networking blade of the Azure portal
A virtual network rule per tenant subnet added on the Public access tab of the server
A separate private endpoint per tenant database, approved individually by the SQL admin
cards.answer: Database-level IP firewall rules, created per database with sp_set_database_firewall_rule after the first server-level rule exists
cards.why: Server-level rules are stored in master and grant a passing address access to every database the server manages, so they cannot isolate tenants; database-level rules live inside each database and are checked first, which is exactly the isolation requirement. Narrowing the server-level list is the nearest wrong answer because the ranges get more precise but any allowed address still reaches all forty databases. Note the operational catch: database-level rules can only be created and managed through Transact-SQL, and only after a server-level rule has been configured by someone with Azure-level permissions.
cards.citation: Azure SQL Database IP firewall rules · outline 2.2

cards.q: A hospital trust hosts its patient portal in Azure App Service and its records database in Azure SQL Database. To get the portal connecting quickly, a contractor set the server firewall's Allow Azure services and resources exception to ON. The security lead reviews the change and objects. What is the accurate statement of the exposure, and the recommended replacement?
options: The setting adds a firewall rule spanning 0.0.0.0 to 0.0.0.0 that admits any Azure resource, including ones in other customers' subscriptions, so replace it with a private endpoint or a virtual network rule
The setting grants access only to Azure resources inside the same subscription, so it is acceptable once the App Service outbound IPs are pinned
The setting disables the server firewall entirely, so public network access must be set to Disable and re-enabled per client
The setting bypasses Microsoft Entra authentication for Azure-hosted callers, so Microsoft Entra-only authentication must be turned on to compensate
cards.answer: The setting adds a firewall rule spanning 0.0.0.0 to 0.0.0.0 that admits any Azure resource, including ones in other customers' subscriptions, so replace it with a private endpoint or a virtual network rule
cards.why: Switching the setting on writes a server-level rule named AllowAllWindowsAzureIps with start and end address 0.0.0.0, and it admits communications from everything inside the Azure boundary regardless of subscription or resource group. The tempting wrong answer is the subscription-scoped reading: it feels like an Azure-internal permission, but nothing about the rule is tied to your tenant, which is why the docs point at virtual network service endpoint rules or Private Link instead. The setting also does not touch authentication, so credentials and database principals remain the only other control.
cards.citation: Azure SQL Database network access controls and IP firewall rules · outline 2.2

cards.q: A retail bank must satisfy an auditor who insists the bank, not Microsoft, controls the key that protects data at rest for eleven databases on one logical server in Azure SQL Database. The DBA proposes rotating each database's encryption key by hand every quarter. What is the correct design, and where does the key sit?
options: Configure customer-managed transparent data encryption so an asymmetric key in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM acts as the TDE protector, set at the server level and inherited by its databases
Configure Always Encrypted with column master keys in Azure Key Vault so the bank holds the keys for every column in all eleven databases
Disable service-managed TDE and enable Azure Storage infrastructure encryption with a customer-managed key on the underlying storage
Enable database-level ledger on each database so every change is cryptographically attested with a bank-held signing key
cards.answer: Configure customer-managed transparent data encryption so an asymmetric key in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM acts as the TDE protector, set at the server level and inherited by its databases
cards.why: Customer-managed TDE, also called bring your own key, replaces the built-in server certificate with a customer-held asymmetric key that wraps each database encryption key and never leaves the vault, and for Azure SQL Database the protector is a server-level property inherited by every database beneath it. Always Encrypted is the closest wrong option and it does give the bank key custody, but it protects designated columns from privileged users rather than satisfying an at-rest requirement across whole databases, and it does not replace the TDE protector. Worth knowing the failure mode: if the server's permissions on the key vault are revoked, the databases become inaccessible while the data stays encrypted.
cards.citation: Transparent data encryption for Azure SQL · outline 2.2

cards.q: A university wants every connection to its student records instance of Azure SQL Managed Instance to come from a Microsoft Entra identity, with no password-based logins accepted. The identity engineer holds the SQL Security Manager role and finds the Microsoft Entra authentication only toggle greyed out in the portal. What is missing, and what happens to the existing SQL logins once it is switched on?
options: A Microsoft Entra administrator has not been assigned on the instance; once set, enabling the toggle blocks SQL authentication logins from connecting while leaving the accounts in place
The SQL Security Manager role cannot enable the setting at all; a SQL Server Contributor must enable it, after which SQL logins are dropped from the instance
Microsoft Entra logins must first be created for every user with CREATE LOGIN FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER; the toggle then deletes any SQL authentication account that has no Entra equivalent

Public network access must be disabled first, because Microsoft Entra-only authentication is available only over private endpoints, and existing SQL logins keep working from inside the virtual network
cards.answer: A Microsoft Entra administrator has not been assigned on the instance; once set, enabling the toggle blocks SQL authentication logins from connecting while leaving the accounts in place
cards.why: The Microsoft Entra admin is a prerequisite: with no admin set the Microsoft Entra authentication only setting stays inactive, and API calls to enable it fail as well. Enabling it disables SQL authentication at the server or instance level, but it does not remove the existing logins and users, it only stops them connecting. The nearest wrong option flips the role split: SQL Security Manager is precisely the role that can set the Entra-only flag, while SQL Server Contributor can set or remove the Entra admin but cannot toggle Entra-only, which is the separation of duties the platform is enforcing.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra-only authentication with Azure SQL · outline 2.2

cards.q: A car parts manufacturer is told by its assessor to prove no client reaches its Azure SQL Database over an obsolete TLS version before the platform team enforces a minimum. Some plant-floor applications use unmaintained drivers and nobody knows what they negotiate. What is the sound sequence, and how does the team gather the evidence?
options: Leave the minimum TLS version unset while identifying clients from the Successful connections metric filtered by TLS version and from the audit file's client_tls_version_name column, then set the minimum to 1.2
Set the minimum TLS version to 1.3 immediately, then read the resulting Error 47072 login failures from the activity log to find the stragglers
Set the connection policy to Proxy so the gateway downgrades legacy clients transparently, then raise the minimum TLS version once every plant is migrated
Enable Advanced Threat Protection and wait for insecure protocol alerts, which name each client that negotiated an obsolete TLS version
cards.answer: Leave the minimum TLS version unset while identifying clients from the Successful connections metric filtered by TLS version and from the audit file's client_tls_version_name column, then set the minimum to 1.2
cards.why: Microsoft's guidance for workloads on unknown or unmaintained drivers is to not set a minimum until you know what clients negotiate, and the two supported discovery routes are the portal metric for successful connections filtered by TLS version and the client_tls_version_name column returned from the audit file. Jumping straight to a minimum of 1.3 is the nearest wrong answer and it does produce login failures, but it takes production down to gather the data and drivers plus operating systems vary in TLS 1.3 support. Remember also that once a minimum is enforced you cannot revert to the default of allowing all supported versions.
cards.citation: Azure SQL Database connectivity settings · outline 2.2

cards.q: A logistics operator has migrated a claims application onto Azure SQL Managed Instance and must land audit records in a blob container it controls, in the same region as the instance. The DBA opens the instance in the portal expecting the same Auditing blade used for Azure SQL Database and cannot find it. What actually configures this?
options: Create a credential named for the container URL with a shared access signature identity, then CREATE SERVER AUDIT to that URL and add a server or database audit specification before setting the audit state on
Turn on Auditing on the instance blade, choose Storage, and pick managed identity as the storage authentication type
Add a diagnostic setting on the instance for SQLSecurityAuditEvents with the storage account as destination
Enable Microsoft Defender for SQL on the instance, which writes its audit trail to the storage account created for vulnerability assessment results
cards.answer: Create a credential named for the container URL with a shared access signature identity, then CREATE SERVER AUDIT to that URL and add a server or database audit specification before setting the audit state on
cards.why: Managed Instance uses SQL Server Audit, so auditing to blob storage is built in Transact-SQL: a credential holding the SAS secret, a server audit targeting the container URL with an optional retention in days, then a server or database audit specification, then ALTER SERVER AUDIT with state on. The diagnostic setting answer is the closest miss, because that route is real but it is how you send Managed Instance audit events to Event Hubs or a Log Analytics workspace, and it still requires a server audit created to EXTERNAL_MONITOR alongside it. The portal Auditing blade with storage authentication types belongs to Azure SQL Database and its logical server, not to Managed Instance.
cards.citation: Azure SQL Managed Instance auditing setup · outline 2.2

cards.q: An insurer moved its Azure SQL Database estate to Microsoft Entra authentication and kept the default audit action groups, including the failed database authentication group. Weeks later the SOC asks for a report of failed sign-in attempts against the claims database and finds almost nothing in the audit logs, even though users complain about rejected sign-ins. What explains this, and where does the evidence live?
options: Failed logins by Microsoft Entra principals are verified before the database is reached, so no audit record is written; those events are recorded in Microsoft Entra sign-in logs in the Microsoft Entra admin center
The failed database authentication group is not honoured on databases using Microsoft Entra authentication and must be replaced with FAILED_LOGIN_GROUP in a database audit specification
Failed logins were captured but silently truncated because the statement field holds at most 4,000 characters, so the records exist with empty statements
Audit records for failed logins are written only to the master folder of the storage container, and the SOC queried the per-database folder
cards.answer: Failed logins by Microsoft Entra principals are verified before the database is reached, so no audit record is written; those events are recorded in Microsoft Entra sign-in logs in the Microsoft Entra admin center
cards.why: With Microsoft Entra logins the gateway validates credentials before the requested database is opened, so a failure never touches the database and nothing is audited; with SQL logins the credentials are checked at the requested database, which is why those failures do appear. Successful sign-ins are audited in both cases. The truncation option is the nearest trap because the 4,000 character limit on the statement field is real, but it clips long statements rather than suppressing whole login records, and it would not explain missing rows.
cards.citation: Auditing in Azure SQL Database and Synapse Analytics · outline 2.2

cards.q: A regulated energy trader must keep Azure SQL Database audit logs tamper-proof for seven years, and its own retention slider on the auditing configuration is currently at 30 days. The storage lead plans a time-based immutability policy on the audit container. What must be true for auditing to keep writing successfully?
options: Allow protected append writes must be set to append blobs or to block and append blobs, and the storage account's retention period must expire sooner than the SQL auditing retention setting
Allow protected append writes must be set to None so the policy cannot be circumvented, and SQL auditing retention must be left at 0 for unlimited retention
The container must use a legal hold rather than a time-based policy, because SQL auditing rewrites existing blobs as new events arrive
The storage account must be general-purpose v1 with a hierarchical namespace so append operations bypass the immutability policy
cards.answer: Allow protected append writes must be set to append blobs or to block and append blobs, and the storage account's retention period must expire sooner than the SQL auditing retention setting
cards.why: Audit logs are written to append blobs, so an immutable container has to permit protected append writes; the None option is explicitly unsupported, which is what makes the second choice the sharpest distractor. For time-based policies the storage account's retention period must expire sooner than the SQL auditing retention value, and a configuration where a storage policy exists while SQL auditing retention remains 0 is not supported. Also worth remembering that changing retention from 0 to a finite value applies only to logs written after the change.
cards.citation: Auditing for Azure SQL Database, immutable log store remarks · outline 2.2

cards.q: A ticketing startup runs its booking store on Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server on the burstable tier, a reporting copy on Azure Database for MySQL flexible server, and an Azure Cosmos DB account for session state. The new security hire wants brute force and anomalous access alerts on all three without buying anything unnecessary. What should be enabled?
options: Turn the Databases plan on for the subscription, which activates Defender for Open-Source Relational Databases for both flexible servers and Defender for Azure Cosmos DB for the account
Enable Defender for Azure SQL Databases at the subscription level, since it covers all Azure-hosted database engines including PostgreSQL, MySQL and Cosmos DB
Enable Defender for SQL Servers on Machines and onboard the flexible servers through Azure Arc, then enable Cosmos DB protection separately
Enable Defender for Open-Source Relational Databases only, because Azure Cosmos DB accounts are protected automatically once any Defender for Databases plan is on
cards.answer: Turn the Databases plan on for the subscription, which activates Defender for Open-Source Relational Databases for both flexible servers and Defender for Azure Cosmos DB for the account
cards.why: Defender for Databases is an umbrella over four separately priced offerings, and enabling the plan on the subscription activates all of them across supported resources, including flexible server PostgreSQL and MySQL at all pricing tiers under the open-source relational databases plan and the Cosmos DB account under its own plan. The last option is the closest miss: the open-source plan genuinely covers the two flexible servers, but Cosmos DB is a distinct plan and is not swept in by enabling a sibling. Defender for Azure SQL Databases protects Azure SQL, managed instances and Synapse dedicated pools, not open-source engines, and Defender for SQL Servers on Machines targets SQL Server on VMs and Arc-enabled SQL Server.
cards.citation: Protect your databases with Defender for Databases and Defender for Open-Source Relational Databases · outline 2.2

cards.q: A media group has SQL vulnerability assessment running in the classic configuration on sixty databases, each pointing at a customer-managed storage account that the platform team is tired of maintaining. They want to move to express configuration. What should they expect from the switch?
options: Defender for Cloud manages scan result storage in the same region as the logical server and no storage account is needed, but existing baselines and scan history are not carried over
The storage account is still required for baselines, and only the recurring scan schedule moves under Microsoft management
Express configuration supports policy scope at subscription, server and database level, so per-database exceptions configured today migrate unchanged
Express configuration is available only for Azure SQL Database, so the managed instances in the estate must remain on classic
cards.answer: Defender for Cloud manages scan result storage in the same region as the logical server and no storage account is needed, but existing baselines and scan history are not carried over
cards.why: Express configuration is the recommended mode: Defender for Cloud holds the results, no customer storage account is involved, results stay in the logical server's region, and the migration notice is explicit that baselines and scan history do not migrate. The policy scope option is the nearest wrong answer because per-database scope is a genuine capability, but it belongs to the classic model; express supports subscription and server scope only. Express configuration is also generally available on Azure SQL Managed Instance and Synapse workspaces, not just Azure SQL Database, so the estate does not have to stay split.
cards.citation: Scan your Azure SQL databases for vulnerabilities, configuration model comparison · outline 2.2

cards.q: It is 02:40. Defender for Cloud has just raised a potential SQL injection alert on the payments database of a retailer's Azure SQL Database, and a second alert reports an unusual export of a large result set by the web application's identity. The on-call engineer has portal access and the database is still serving traffic. What is the containment move right now?
options: Open the alert in Defender for Cloud to read the exploited statement and the MITRE tactic it maps to, correlate the timeframe against the SQL audit log, and act on the alert's recommended mitigation for the affected principal
Switch the logical server's minimum TLS version to 1.3 to break the attacker's session, then investigate in the morning
Disable auditing on the payments database so the attacker cannot see what is being recorded, then rotate the SQL administrator password
Enable dynamic data masking on the payment columns so the in-flight queries return masked values
cards.answer: Open the alert in Defender for Cloud to read the exploited statement and the MITRE tactic it maps to, correlate the timeframe against the SQL audit log, and act on the alert's recommended mitigation for the affected principal
cards.why: Advanced Threat Protection alerts are action-oriented: for SQL injection the alert carries the vulnerable statement that was exploited, plus the tactic and recommended investigation and mitigation steps, and auditing exists precisely to give the full investigation trail alongside it. Enabling dynamic data masking mid-incident is the nearest plausible wrong move, because masking is a real Azure SQL control, but it obscures results for non-privileged callers rather than stopping an injected statement running under the application's own principal, and it changes application behaviour under load. Disabling auditing during an incident destroys the evidence you are about to need.
cards.citation: SQL Advanced Threat Protection and Microsoft Defender for SQL · outline 2.2

cards.q: During a live investigation into suspected insider access at a pension fund, the SOC queries the Log Analytics workspace for SQLSecurityAuditEvents from the annuities database and gets rows up to nine days ago, then nothing. Auditing still shows as ON in the database blade and no error was ever raised. What has happened, and what restores the flow?
options: The diagnostic settings resource created for the audit target was deleted, which fails auditing silently; re-save the auditing configuration to recreate it and add an alert on diagnostic setting deletion
The Log Analytics workspace hit its daily ingestion cap, so re-saving the auditing configuration will not help until the cap is raised
Server-level auditing overrode the database-level policy nine days ago, so the events are in the master folder of the storage container instead
The audit retention slider expired the recent logs; set retention to 0 for unlimited retention and the missing nine days will reappear
cards.answer: The diagnostic settings resource created for the audit target was deleted, which fails auditing silently; re-save the auditing configuration to recreate it and add an alert on diagnostic setting deletion
cards.why: When auditing targets an external monitor such as Log Analytics or Event Hubs, a diagnostic settings resource named for SQLSecurityAuditEvents is created and is critical to the pipeline; if it is deleted, intentionally or not, auditing fails silently and no logs reach the target, which matches an ON toggle with no events and no error. The server-versus-database option is the closest wrong answer, because server and database audits genuinely coexist and the redesigned server audit does consolidate into a master folder, but that is a storage destination behaviour and would not stop workspace ingestion. Retention never removes only the newest logs, and a change from unlimited retention applies forward, not backward.
cards.citation: Set up Auditing for Azure SQL Database, Event Hubs and Log Analytics destinations · outline 2.2

cards.q: A telecoms provider is watching credentials for a reporting account being used from an unfamiliar hosting range against the public endpoint of its Azure SQL Database logical server, right now. All legitimate consumers already reach the server through an approved private endpoint in the core virtual network. The incident commander wants the public path shut immediately. What happens when they set Deny public network access on the server?
options: All connections from public endpoints are refused with an error stating the public network interface is not accessible, only private endpoint traffic survives, and firewall rules cannot be added or edited until public access is re-enabled
Existing sessions from public addresses continue until they end, and new public connections fall back to the private endpoint automatically
The server keeps accepting public connections from addresses already listed in server-level firewall rules, since explicit rules take precedence over the deny setting
Private endpoint clients must switch their connection strings to the private link FQDN of the server, since the public FQDN stops resolving
cards.answer: All connections from public endpoints are refused with an error stating the public network interface is not accessible, only private endpoint traffic survives, and firewall rules cannot be added or edited until public access is re-enabled
cards.why: With public network access disabled, only private endpoint connections are allowed and public attempts fail with the not-accessible error, and any attempt to add, remove or edit firewall rules is refused as well, so the containment is decisive but it also freezes your firewall administration until you set the server back to selected networks. The precedence answer is the seductive one: firewall rules do not survive the deny setting, they are simply unreachable. And clients must keep using the ordinary server FQDN even over Private Link, because logins made to the private IP or to the privatelink FQDN fail by design.
cards.citation: Azure SQL Database connectivity settings and Azure Private Link for Azure SQL Database · outline 2.2

cards.q: A payments processor is mid-incident on its Azure SQL Managed Instance when the forensics lead reports the audit trail stopped overnight: no new blobs are landing in the audit container, and the server audit for the instance was created to a container URL. The credential for that URL was created a year ago at go-live. What is the most likely cause and the fix?
options: The shared access signature in the credential reached its end date, so auditing to the URL fails; generate a new SAS, recreate the credential for the container URL, and confirm the server audit state is on
The instance's system-assigned managed identity lost its Storage Blob Data Contributor assignment on that account, so grant it again and re-save the auditing configuration in the portal
The container's public access level was left as Private, which blocks the instance from appending blobs; set it to blob-level anonymous read access
The server audit specification was created without the batch completed group, so events are collected but never written to the container
cards.answer: The shared access signature in the credential reached its end date, so auditing to the URL fails; generate a new SAS, recreate the credential for the container URL, and confirm the server audit state is on
cards.why: Managed Instance auditing to blob storage authenticates through a credential holding a SAS token with an explicit end date, and the guidance is blunt that the token must be renewed on expiry to avoid audit failures, which fits an audit that simply stops writing a year after go-live. The managed identity answer is the closest wrong option because that mechanism is real, but it belongs to the logical server auditing path for Azure SQL Database writing to storage that sits behind a virtual network or firewall, not to the Managed Instance credential and URL path. Private is the correct public access level for an audit container, and a missing action group would leave no events collected at all rather than an abrupt stop.
cards.citation: Azure SQL Managed Instance auditing setup · outline 2.2

cards.q: After an incident in which a database administrator at a building society was able to edit the audit configuration and then read the audit blobs, the review board asks for a control design that would have prevented it. Two DBAs currently hold Owner on the subscription and Storage Blob Data Owner on the audit storage account. What should the hardening pass put in place?
options: Split the duties: leave Microsoft Entra admin assignment with SQL Server Contributor, keep security settings such as Microsoft Entra-only authentication with SQL Security Manager, and restrict the audit storage account to auditors rather than DBAs
Grant both DBAs the SQL Security Manager role in addition to Owner, so security settings and audit targets are managed under one accountable role
Move audit logs to the same subscription as the databases and give the DBAs Storage Blob Data Reader only, since read access to audit blobs is harmless
Replace auditing with vulnerability assessment in express configuration, because Defender for Cloud stores those results where DBAs cannot reach them
cards.answer: Split the duties: leave Microsoft Entra admin assignment with SQL Server Contributor, keep security settings such as Microsoft Entra-only authentication with SQL Security Manager, and restrict the audit storage account to auditors rather than DBAs
cards.why: Azure SQL splits these deliberately: SQL Server Contributor can set or remove the Microsoft Entra admin but cannot toggle Microsoft Entra-only authentication, while SQL Security Manager can set the security flag but not the admin, and the auditing guidance adds that access to the audit storage account should be restricted so that DBAs are separated from auditors. Consolidating both under one role is the nearest wrong answer and it is exactly the anti-pattern the split exists to prevent. Read-only access to audit blobs is not harmless either, since audit records can expose the sensitive values that were queried, which is why the guidance pairs restricted audit access with encryption of sensitive data.
cards.citation: Playbook for common security requirements with Azure SQL and Microsoft Entra-only authentication permissions · outline 2.2

cards.q: A manufacturer's post-incident review finds that the compromised database was a SQL Server 2019 instance on an Azure VM that nobody had onboarded, while the twelve Azure SQL databases beside it were all covered. The team wants coverage that does not depend on someone remembering to enable a plan per resource. What should the recovery turn set up?
options: Enable the Databases plan at the subscription level so newly created resources are protected automatically, turn on SQL Servers on Machines within it, and confirm coverage with the Defender for Cloud coverage workbook
Enable Defender for Azure SQL Databases at the subscription level, since SQL Server on Azure VMs is protected by that plan once the VM is in the same subscription
Enable Defender for SQL at the resource level on each SQL virtual machine, because subscription-level enablement does not reach machines
Assign the Azure Policy that configures Defender for Azure Cosmos DB, which enrols every database resource type in the subscription
cards.answer: Enable the Databases plan at the subscription level so newly created resources are protected automatically, turn on SQL Servers on Machines within it, and confirm coverage with the Defender for Cloud coverage workbook
cards.why: Subscription-level enablement is the recommended pattern precisely because future resources on that subscription are protected as they are created, and the coverage workbook exists to show which plans are on across subscriptions and resources. SQL Server on an Azure VM is covered by the SQL Servers on Machines plan, selected under Select types within the Databases plan, not by Defender for Azure SQL Databases, which makes the second option the closest miss. Resource-level enablement for machines is possible but the docs frame it as the exception, and it requires disabling the plan on the subscription first, reintroducing the very gap the review is trying to close.
cards.citation: Protect your databases with Defender for Databases and Enable Defender for SQL Servers on Machines · outline 2.2

cards.q: A grocery retailer runs a three-tier ordering app in one virtual network. Web VMs, business-logic VMs and SQL VMs all scale in and out overnight, so their private IP addresses churn. The security team wants a single subnet-level NSG that permits port 1433 only from the logic tier to the database tier, and blocks every other source, without anyone editing IP lists again. What should the engineer build?
options: Put the logic-tier NICs in one application security group and the database-tier NICs in another, then write an allow rule on 1433 with the logic group as source and the database group as destination, above a broader deny rule for the database group
Create an IP group in Azure Firewall for each tier and reference those IP groups from the NSG rules on the database subnet
Tag each virtual machine with its tier name and use an Azure Policy definition to generate matching NSG rules whenever a VM is created
Reference the VirtualNetwork service tag as the source of the allow rule and rely on the AllowVNetInBound default rule for the rest
cards.answer: Put the logic-tier NICs in one application security group and the database-tier NICs in another, then write an allow rule on 1433 with the logic group as source and the database group as destination, above a broader deny rule for the database group
cards.why: Application security groups let NSG rules name a group of network interfaces rather than addresses, so membership follows the VM through any scaling event and the rule text never changes. The closest wrong answer is the VirtualNetwork service tag: that tag covers the whole address space, so it would readmit the web tier and anything else in the network, which is the opposite of the tier isolation being asked for. Azure Firewall IP groups are a firewall construct and cannot be selected as an NSG source or destination.
cards.citation: Microsoft Learn, Application security groups and Azure network security groups overview - outline 2.3

cards.q: An industrial manufacturer discovers that any VM in its plant virtual network can reach the historian database subnet on port 1433, because nobody wrote a rule for it. An engineer opens the subnet NSG, finds the entry named AllowVNetInBound at priority 65000, and tries to delete it. The portal refuses. What is the correct way to close the path?
options: Add a custom inbound deny rule for TCP 1433 at a priority number lower than 65000, then add a higher priority allow rule for only the plant application subnet
Delete the default rule through Azure PowerShell, since only the portal blocks removal of default security rules
Set the subnet NSG to deny by default by turning off the default rule set in the NSG properties blade
Raise the priority number of AllowVNetInBound to 65501 so the DenyAllInbound default rule is evaluated first
cards.answer: Add a custom inbound deny rule for TCP 1433 at a priority number lower than 65000, then add a higher priority allow rule for only the plant application subnet
cards.why: Azure default security rules cannot be deleted or reprioritised in any tooling; they sit at the highest numbers so custom rules always win, and rules are processed lowest number first with processing stopping on the first match. The nearest wrong option is renumbering AllowVNetInBound, which is impossible for the same reason deletion is, and would in any case still leave the flow allowed. Deleting through PowerShell fails identically because the restriction is in the platform, not the portal.
cards.citation: Microsoft Learn, Azure network security groups overview, default security rules - outline 2.3

cards.q: A university has 140 virtual networks across a dozen faculty subscriptions. Central IT deploys an Azure Virtual Network Manager security admin configuration whose rule collection denies inbound TCP 3389 at priority 10 for every network group. The astronomy department genuinely needs RDP into one research network from a jump host range. What is the supported way to carve out that exception?
options: Add a second rule collection targeting a network group that contains only the research network, with an Allow or Always allow rule at a priority between 1 and 9
Ask the astronomy admins to create an NSG allow rule for 3389 at priority 100 on the research subnet, since NSG rules are evaluated before security admin rules
Raise the deny rule to priority 4096 so that any NSG rule in a member virtual network takes precedence over it
Remove the research virtual network from Azure Virtual Network Manager scope and manage it entirely with NSGs and Azure Firewall
cards.answer: Add a second rule collection targeting a network group that contains only the research network, with an Allow or Always allow rule at a priority between 1 and 9
cards.why: Security admin rules use 1 to 4096 with the lower number winning, so an exception must carry a smaller priority number than the blanket deny, and it is delivered as another rule collection aimed at a narrower network group. The closest wrong option is the NSG allow rule: security admin rules are evaluated before NSG rules, and a Deny action ends evaluation without ever reaching the NSG, so the faculty rule would never be consulted. Priority 4096 is the weakest priority, not a bypass.
cards.citation: Microsoft Learn, Virtual Network Manager security admin rules; blocking high-risk ports - outline 2.3

cards.q: A logistics operator runs Azure Virtual WAN with two hubs, each converted to a secured hub by adding Azure Firewall. Weeks later an audit finds that traffic between a branch site and a spoke network in the same hub, and traffic between the two hubs, is flowing without ever hitting a firewall. Internet-bound traffic is being inspected correctly. What was missed?
options: A private traffic routing policy was never configured as part of routing intent on each hub, so only internet traffic was being forwarded to the firewall
The hubs are Basic Virtual WAN, and branch to spoke inspection requires the Standard type
User defined routes pointing at the firewall private IP address were not applied to each spoke subnet
The firewall policy inherits from a parent policy, and inherited network rule collections do not apply to branch traffic
cards.answer: A private traffic routing policy was never configured as part of routing intent on each hub, so only internet traffic was being forwarded to the firewall
cards.why: Routing intent has two independent policies, and the private traffic policy is what forces branch to branch, branch to virtual network and inter-hub flows through the next hop security solution, including inside a single hub. The nearest wrong answer is user defined routes: a secured hub provides automated routing, and hand-written UDRs on spokes are exactly what routing intent removes the need for. The Basic type is a distractor about gateway scale, not inspection.
cards.citation: Microsoft Learn, Virtual WAN routing intent; secured virtual hub - outline 2.3

cards.q: A hospital trust wants clinicians on unmanaged home laptops to reach a small internal application over point-to-site VPN, and wants sign-in governed by Conditional Access with multifactor authentication rather than by distributing certificates. The existing gateway is a Basic SKU policy-based VPN gateway created years ago. What must change before Microsoft Entra ID authentication will work?
options: Rebuild the gateway as a route-based VPN gateway on a SKU above Basic and configure the tunnel type as OpenVPN with Microsoft Entra ID as the authentication type
Keep the existing gateway and add IKEv2 as a second tunnel type, since Microsoft Entra ID authentication rides over IKEv2
Keep the existing gateway and configure RADIUS authentication pointed at a domain controller synchronised to Microsoft Entra ID
Convert the policy-based gateway to route-based in place, then select SSTP as the tunnel type for Microsoft Entra ID authentication
cards.answer: Rebuild the gateway as a route-based VPN gateway on a SKU above Basic and configure the tunnel type as OpenVPN with Microsoft Entra ID as the authentication type
cards.why: Point-to-site requires a route-based gateway, Microsoft Entra ID authentication is supported only over the OpenVPN protocol with the Azure VPN Client, and the Basic SKU plus policy-based types are explicitly incompatible. The closest wrong option adds IKEv2: if you select both tunnel types, Entra ID sign-in still binds only to the OpenVPN tunnel, so IKEv2 clients would fall back to another method. A policy-based gateway also cannot be converted in place; it must be deleted and recreated.
cards.citation: Microsoft Learn, About Point-to-Site VPN; P2S gateway with Entra ID authentication - outline 2.3

cards.q: An insurer has replaced its VPN with Microsoft Entra Private Access and put the whole data centre range 10.20.0.0/16 on ports 22, 443 and 3389 into Quick Access. The claims payment server at 10.20.7.9 must now be reachable only by a small approved team under a stricter Conditional Access policy. An engineer creates a Global Secure Access enterprise application with a segment for 10.20.7.9 on port 3389. What else is required for the tighter control to actually bite?
options: Assign the approved users or groups directly to the new enterprise application, and remove 10.20.7.9 from the Quick Access range by splitting it into smaller blocks
Nothing further, because Quick Access assignments and Conditional Access policies are inherited automatically by any overlapping enterprise application
Delete the Quick Access application entirely, because a tenant cannot run Quick Access and per-app access at the same time
Install a dedicated private network connector on the payment server itself, since per-app access requires a connector inside the target host
cards.answer: Assign the approved users or groups directly to the new enterprise application, and remove 10.20.7.9 from the Quick Access range by splitting it into smaller blocks
cards.why: An overlapping segment on an enterprise application takes priority over Quick Access, but access assignments do not carry across, so users who worked through Quick Access are blocked until they are assigned to the new app, and nested groups are not honoured. Microsoft also advises removing the moved segment from Quick Access, which means breaking the wide subnet into smaller ranges. The closest wrong answer claims automatic inheritance, which is precisely the trap that locks users out.
cards.citation: Microsoft Learn, Global Secure Access per-app access configuration - outline 2.3

cards.q: A retail bank must stop payment reconciliation data traversing public addressing. The storage account holds settlement files in blob containers and a mounted share used by a legacy reporting job. An engineer creates one private endpoint against the storage account with the blob target subresource and links the matching private DNS zone. The reporting job still fails to mount the share privately. What is the correct fix?
options: Create a second private endpoint against the same storage account with the file target subresource and link its own private DNS zone
Add the file service to the existing private endpoint by editing its target subresource list to include both blob and file
Enable a service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage on the reporting subnet so the file share is reached over the Azure backbone
Create a Private Link service in the storage subscription and point the reporting job at the generated alias
cards.answer: Create a second private endpoint against the same storage account with the file target subresource and link its own private DNS zone
cards.why: A private endpoint maps to a single target subresource, so storage needs separate endpoints for blob, file, queue and the rest, each with its own DNS zone; Microsoft warns against putting records for different services in one zone. The nearest wrong option is editing the existing endpoint, which cannot hold multiple subresources. A service endpoint would work over the backbone but keeps the public address and the public front door, which is exactly what the bank is trying to remove.
cards.citation: Microsoft Learn, What is a private endpoint and Azure Private Endpoint private DNS zone values - outline 2.3

cards.q: A software firm publishes its claims-processing API to insurer customers through an Azure Private Link service in front of a standard load balancer. Two named customer subscriptions should connect with no human in the loop; anyone else who somehow obtains the alias must not even be able to raise a request. How should the provider configure the service?
options: Set visibility to a restricted set of the two customer subscriptions, and add those same subscriptions to the auto-approval list
Leave visibility set to anyone with the alias, and add the two customer subscriptions to the auto-approval list so all other requests stay pending
Set visibility to role-based access control only, and grant the customers a reader role on the load balancer frontend IP configuration
Publish the service with eight NAT IP configurations and enable TCP proxy v2 so only recognised consumer source addresses are accepted
cards.answer: Set visibility to a restricted set of the two customer subscriptions, and add those same subscriptions to the auto-approval list
cards.why: Visibility controls who is even exposed to the service, while auto-approval controls which of those exposed subscriptions connect without manual action; the requirement names both, so both must be set. The closest wrong option leaves visibility open to anyone with the alias, which still lets strangers create pending requests and leaks the existence of the service. TCP proxy v2 only surfaces consumer connection details to the backend; it is not an access control.
cards.citation: Microsoft Learn, What is Azure Private Link service, control service exposure and control service access - outline 2.3

cards.q: A fashion retailer routes spoke egress through Azure Firewall using a firewall policy. A network rule collection at priority 200 allows TCP 443 to any destination. An application rule collection denies the FQDN of a file-sharing site. Data loss prevention reports staff are still uploading to that site over HTTPS. Why is the application rule not stopping them, and what changes it?
options: Network rules are always processed before application rules, so the broad 443 allow matches first and terminates processing; tighten or remove that network rule so the flow reaches the application rules
Application rules are only evaluated for inbound traffic, so outbound blocking of an FQDN requires a DNAT rule collection instead
The application rule collection sits in a rule collection group with a higher priority number, so moving it below 200 will make it match first
FQDN filtering over HTTPS requires the Basic SKU to be upgraded to Standard, because Standard is the first SKU with any application rule support
cards.answer: Network rules are always processed before application rules, so the broad 443 allow matches first and terminates processing; tighten or remove that network rule so the flow reaches the application rules
cards.why: Azure Firewall processes DNAT, then network, then application rules regardless of collection or group priority, and rules are terminating, so a wide network allow on 443 short-circuits every FQDN decision behind it. The nearest wrong option is reordering priorities, which cannot override the fixed rule-type ordering. Application rule support with FQDN filtering based on SNI exists even in the Basic SKU, so a SKU change is not the issue.
cards.citation: Microsoft Learn, Configure Azure Firewall rules, rule processing logic - outline 2.3

cards.q: An energy utility cannot explain why a SCADA reporting VM is refused on TCP 8080. There is an NSG on the VM network interface, another on its subnet, and central IT also manages the virtual network with Azure Virtual Network Manager. The on-call engineer needs one view that shows every rule actually acting on that interface, and which one wins. Which Network Watcher capability should they open?
options: Effective security rules, which aggregates the interface NSG, the subnet NSG and the Virtual Network Manager admin rules applied to that virtual network
Connection troubleshoot, which tests the path at a point in time and reports latency and hop-by-hop results
Next hop, which returns the next hop type, address and route table identifier for the destination
Traffic analytics, which visualises flow log data and shows denied conversations by source address
cards.answer: Effective security rules, which aggregates the interface NSG, the subnet NSG and the Virtual Network Manager admin rules applied to that virtual network
cards.why: Effective security rules is the aggregated inbound and outbound view for a network interface, and it explicitly includes security admin rules delivered by Azure Virtual Network Manager alongside both NSGs, with a CSV download for audit evidence. The closest wrong answer is Traffic analytics, which reports what already happened in flow logs rather than the current rule set, so it cannot prove which rule is winning right now. Next hop diagnoses routing, not filtering.
cards.citation: Microsoft Learn, Effective security rules overview and Azure Network Watcher overview - outline 2.3

cards.q: It is 02:10. Azure Firewall Premium on the payments hub is logging repeated IDPS signature matches for a command and control family, sourced from three VMs in the card-processing spoke, and the sessions are completing. The firewall policy has IDPS enabled in alert mode and threat intelligence set to alert only. The incident lead wants the beaconing stopped in the next few minutes without cutting the whole spoke off. What is the containment move?
options: Switch the policy IDPS mode to alert and deny so the engine works inline and drops matching sessions, and set threat intelligence to alert and deny
Add a network rule collection at priority 100 denying all outbound traffic from the card-processing spoke address range
Add the three VM addresses to the IDPS bypass list so the engine stops generating repeated alerts for them
Enable TLS inspection on the outbound application rules so the encrypted beacons can be decrypted before any decision is taken
cards.answer: Switch the policy IDPS mode to alert and deny so the engine works inline and drops matching sessions, and set threat intelligence to alert and deny
cards.why: In alert mode the IDPS engine runs in parallel with rule processing and only records; in alert and deny it works inline after the rules engine and blocks matching flows, which is the surgical stop for signature-confirmed traffic. The nearest wrong option is the blanket outbound deny, which halts card processing entirely and is a bigger outage than the incident. The bypass list is the exact opposite of containment, since it excludes those addresses from filtering.
cards.citation: Microsoft Learn, Azure Firewall Premium features, IDPS, and Azure Firewall threat intelligence-based filtering - outline 2.3

cards.q: A ransomware operator has a foothold on a build agent and is spreading over SMB on TCP 445 into neighbouring virtual networks across four subscriptions. Each application team owns its own NSGs and several have allow rules for 445 that they will not change quickly. Central IT already runs an Azure Virtual Network Manager instance scoped to the management group with the security admin feature enabled. What stops the spread fastest and holds?
options: Create a security admin rule collection with a Deny rule for inbound TCP 445 targeting the network group that holds those virtual networks, then deploy the configuration to their regions
Create a security admin rule collection with an Allow rule for inbound TCP 445 at priority 1 so it is evaluated before the team NSG rules
Ask each application team to raise a deny rule for 445 at priority 100 in their subnet NSGs and confirm by inspecting effective security rules
Apply an Azure Policy deny effect on new NSG rules that permit port 445 across the four subscriptions
cards.answer: Create a security admin rule collection with a Deny rule for inbound TCP 445 targeting the network group that holds those virtual networks, then deploy the configuration to their regions
cards.why: Security admin rules outrank NSGs and a Deny action terminates evaluation, so the traffic never reaches the teams conflicting allow rules; deployment to the target regions is what makes the configuration take effect. The closest wrong option is the Allow rule, which is evaluated first but then hands the flow onward to NSG rules, so the permissive team rules would still let SMB through.
