Azure Policy only governs future resource configuration and does nothing to traffic in flight.
cards.citation: Microsoft Learn, Virtual Network Manager security admin rules - outline 2.3

cards.q: A leaked storage account key is being used right now from an unfamiliar internet address to enumerate a blob container holding patient imaging. The account already has a private endpoint for the blob subresource, and the clinical VMs resolve it privately through the linked private DNS zone. The attacker is not on the network. What is the immediate containment step?
options: Set public network access on the storage account to disabled so the service refuses connections that do not arrive through the private endpoint, then rotate the key
Delete the private DNS zone record for the account so the hostname no longer resolves for the attacker
Attach an NSG to the private endpoint subnet with an outbound deny rule aimed at the attacker address range
Reject the private endpoint connection on the storage account and recreate it with manual approval
cards.answer: Set public network access on the storage account to disabled so the service refuses connections that do not arrive through the private endpoint, then rotate the key
cards.why: A private endpoint adds a private path but does not by itself close the public front door; the service keeps accepting internet connections until public network access is turned off, or until the service firewall itself refuses that caller. The nearest wrong answer attacks DNS, but the public CNAME chain is deliberately resolvable from anywhere and removing the private zone would break the clinical VMs while leaving the attacker unaffected. Outbound deny rules on a private endpoint are not a valid scenario, since the service provider never originates traffic.
cards.citation: Microsoft Learn, What is a private endpoint, network security of private endpoints, and private endpoint DNS configuration - outline 2.3

cards.q: A payments platform publishes a settlement API through an Azure Private Link service. During a review this morning the provider sees an approved private endpoint connection from a subscription nobody recognises, and telemetry shows it is actively pulling data. Visibility on the service was left set to anyone with the alias, and the auto-approval list was copied from a spreadsheet. What does the on-call engineer do first?
options: Reject the unrecognised private endpoint connection on the Private Link service, then remove that subscription from auto-approval and tighten visibility to the trusted subscriptions
Delete the Private Link service so the alias becomes invalid, then recreate it after the investigation closes
Add a deny rule for the consumer address range in the NSG on the subnet holding the NAT IP configurations
Enable TCP proxy v2 on the service so the backend can read the consumer source address and reject the session itself
cards.answer: Reject the unrecognised private endpoint connection on the Private Link service, then remove that subscription from auto-approval and tighten visibility to the trusted subscriptions
cards.why: Only approved connections can carry traffic, so rejecting that connection cuts the data path immediately, and fixing auto-approval and visibility stops the same subscription reconnecting. The closest wrong option deletes the service, which severs every legitimate customer at once and is a self-inflicted outage. An NSG on the NAT IP subnet is the wrong lever because consumer traffic is network address translated on arrival, so the original consumer address is not what the rule would see.
cards.citation: Microsoft Learn, What is Azure Private Link service, control service access and NAT IP configuration - outline 2.3

cards.q: After a quiet week the network team reviews the site-to-site tunnel carrying card settlement traffic to a partner data centre. The partner auditor rejects the connection because the negotiated Diffie-Hellman group is too weak for their standard, and demands Group 24 with AES256 and SHA384. The Azure side is a route-based gateway on a modern SKU with several other connections that must not change. What should the team put in place?
options: Create a custom IPsec and IKE policy with the required algorithms and key strengths and apply it to that one connection
Change the gateway SKU to a higher tier, because stronger Diffie-Hellman groups are only offered on the larger gateway sizes
Recreate the gateway as policy-based and use policy-based traffic selectors so the partner device dictates the proposal
Set the connection mode to responder only so the partner device proposes its own stronger parameters during main mode
cards.answer: Create a custom IPsec and IKE policy with the required algorithms and key strengths and apply it to that one connection
cards.why: Azure VPN gateways support per-connection custom IPsec and IKE policy precisely so one tunnel can meet a compliance bar without disturbing the default proposals used by the others; the default sets exist for broad interoperability and lean on weaker groups. The nearest wrong answer is the SKU change, which affects throughput and tunnel counts rather than the cryptographic proposals on offer. Rebuilding as policy-based would strip route-based capabilities and is not how algorithm selection is controlled.
cards.citation: Microsoft Learn, About cryptographic requirements and Azure VPN gateways - outline 2.3

cards.q: A law firm cut over from its legacy VPN to Microsoft Entra Private Access in one weekend by dropping every internal subnet and wildcard domain into Quick Access, and the incident just closed showed a paralegal account reaching a matter management server it had no business touching. During the recovery review, what should the team commit to as the target state?
options: Treat Quick Access as a transition step and move sensitive resources onto per-app enterprise applications with their own segments, user assignments and Conditional Access policies
Keep Quick Access as the single application and rely on Conditional Access policies scoped to user risk to restrict which servers each account can open
Keep Quick Access but split it across several connector groups so each department reaches only the resources served by its own connector
Retire Private Access for sensitive systems and reintroduce the VPN gateway with certificate authentication for those users only
cards.answer: Treat Quick Access as a transition step and move sensitive resources onto per-app enterprise applications with their own segments, user assignments and Conditional Access policies
cards.why: Microsoft positions Quick Access as a transition state for VPN replacement, with application segmentation and granular per-app controls delivered by Global Secure Access enterprise applications, each carrying its own assignments and policies. The closest wrong option leans on Conditional Access alone, but a policy on the single Quick Access app applies to the whole tunnelled range and cannot express which server a given account may reach. Connector groups steer traffic and provide resilience; they are not an authorisation boundary.
cards.citation: Microsoft Learn, Quick Access configuration; Microsoft Entra Private Access concepts - outline 2.3

cards.q: A grocery retailer is two weeks from switching on Microsoft 365 Copilot for 4,000 store managers. The compliance lead wants a repeatable measurement of which SharePoint sites hold sensitive files reachable through broad sharing links, without anyone hand-picking sites first. In the Microsoft Purview portal, what gives her that baseline soonest?
options: Rely on the default data risk assessment under DSPM, which runs weekly across the top 100 SharePoint sites by usage
Build a custom data risk assessment scoped to every site in the tenant and run it on demand
Run the SharePoint Advanced Management site access review on each site collection in turn
Open Activity explorer and filter the AI activities tab for prompts that returned sensitive information types
cards.answer: Rely on the default data risk assessment under DSPM, which runs weekly across the top 100 SharePoint sites by usage
cards.why: The default Microsoft 365 assessment needs no scoping decisions and already covers the busiest hundred sites on a weekly cadence, so it is the fastest route to a baseline of items found, sensitive data detected, and links shared with anyone. A custom assessment is the nearest wrong answer: it is the right tool when you need particular users or sites, but you must define the scope yourself and then wait for results to settle before the numbers mean anything. Activity explorer reports on interactions that already happened rather than on standing exposure.
cards.citation: Microsoft Purview DSPM data risk assessments for oversharing (dspm-oversharing) · outline 3.1

cards.q: A teaching hospital has agents from three sources: declarative agents built in Agent Builder, Copilot Studio agents, and agents registered through Microsoft Agent 365. The security lead opens DSPM and lands on Discover then Apps and agents, but the Agent 365 agents she was told about are missing. Where should she look instead?
options: The AI observability page in DSPM, whose inventory of AI apps and agents does cover Microsoft Agent 365
The Asset explorer Standard tab, which unifies unlabeled and classified data by workload
The Posture page, where key posture metrics and the 30-day trend graph are shown
Remediation actions under Tasks and actions, where automatic policies are listed
cards.answer: The AI observability page in DSPM, whose inventory of AI apps and agents does cover Microsoft Agent 365
cards.why: Discover then Apps and agents deliberately excludes Agent 365 agents; AI observability is the page that covers them, with per-agent activity from the last 30 days and the policies governing each one. Asset explorer is the tempting miss because it also has an Agent tab, but that tab is for the Data Security Posture Agent, not an inventory of your organisation's AI agents. Posture and Remediation actions surface metrics and policies rather than an agent inventory.
cards.citation: Microsoft Purview DSPM overview (dspm-learn-about) · outline 3.1

cards.q: A regional bank wants Defender to inspect and block unsafe tool invocations by its Copilot Studio claims agent while the agent is running, not merely alert afterwards. The security administrator has already onboarded to Agent 365. What must still happen before that runtime blocking works for Copilot Studio?
options: Toggle real-time protection on in Defender and then have a Power Platform administrator finish the onboarding, exchanging a matching App ID
Onboard the agent's host devices to Defender for Endpoint with antivirus in active mode
Register the agent with the Work IQ MCP tooling server so its tool calls become visible to Defender
Assign the agent a distinct Microsoft Entra agent identity so real-time protection rules can be scoped to it
cards.answer: Toggle real-time protection on in Defender and then have a Power Platform administrator finish the onboarding, exchanging a matching App ID
cards.why: Copilot Studio coverage is a two-portal handshake: the security admin enables real-time protection under Settings, Security for AI, and passes a URL to a Power Platform administrator, who completes the external threat provider setup using the same App ID that is then pasted back into Defender. The Work IQ MCP answer is the closest trap because that dependency is real for Agent 365 tool invocations, but Copilot Studio coverage explicitly does not rely on it. Defender for Endpoint onboarding covers local agents running on endpoints, a separate path.
cards.citation: Defender security for AI agents, getting started (get-started-defender-security-for-ai) · outline 3.1

cards.q: An automotive manufacturer has dozens of Foundry agents of the same class, all provisioned from one agent identity blueprint. Governance wants a single Conditional Access policy that covers every current and future agent of that class rather than a policy per agent. Which object should the policy target, and where is the inventory reviewed?
options: The agent identity blueprint, reviewed under Entra ID then Agent ID then All agent identities in the Microsoft Entra admin center
Each individual agent identity service principal, reviewed on the Enterprise applications blade
The Foundry project's managed identity, reviewed on the project Identity pane in the Azure portal
The agent application resource, reviewed in the Agent 365 registry in the Microsoft 365 admin center
cards.answer: The agent identity blueprint, reviewed under Entra ID then Agent ID then All agent identities in the Microsoft Entra admin center
cards.why: The blueprint is the governing template for a class of agents, and classifying agents this way is precisely what lets an administrator apply Conditional Access, revoke permissions, or audit across every identity of that kind at once. Targeting each agent identity individually is the nearest wrong answer: those service principals are the runtime actors and do carry RBAC assignments, but policy applied one by one does not survive the next agent being created. The project managed identity only authenticates the blueprint to Entra ID and is not the principal you govern.
cards.citation: Agent identity concepts in Microsoft Foundry (agent-identity) · outline 3.1

cards.q: After an alert fires on a university's research assistant agent, the SOC must establish how far the compromise reached: which tools the agent invoked, which files it touched, and which identities are implicated. Which Advanced Hunting table in Defender carries the Agent 365 observability data for those agent actions and tool invocations?
options: CloudAppEvents
AgentsInfo
BehaviorInfo
AlertEvidence
cards.answer: CloudAppEvents
cards.why: Agent 365 observability data, meaning the agent's actions, tool invocations, and data access events, lands in CloudAppEvents, which is what root-cause and scope work queries. AgentsInfo is the closest wrong choice and is genuinely useful, but it is an inventory and configuration snapshot table, telling you what the agent is rather than what it did. BehaviorInfo records real-time protection audit and block events specifically, and AlertEvidence lists entities attached to an alert.
cards.citation: Defender AI agent threat detection and investigation (ai-agent-detection-protection) · outline 3.1

cards.q: A logistics firm's Foundry agent read shipment blobs happily all through development. The team publishes it, and every storage call now fails with an authorization error even though nothing about the storage account changed. What is the most likely cause?
options: Publishing created a distinct agent identity, and the storage role assignment still points at the shared project identity
The connection's audience value was left at the MCP server URL rather than the storage resource identifier
The blueprint is still using a client secret credential that expired when the agent was published
The published agent inherited the Microsoft.DefaultV2 guardrail, which blocks outbound tool calls
cards.answer: Publishing created a distinct agent identity, and the storage role assignment still points at the shared project identity
cards.why: Unpublished agents authenticate as the shared project identity; publishing mints a new identity with its own identifier, and role assignments do not carry across, so every permission the agent relied on must be granted again to the new principal. The audience answer is the nearest miss because a wrong audience really does cause authentication failures even with correct roles, but the failure here appeared exactly at publish time with no connection change, which points at the identity swap. Guardrails moderate content and do not revoke storage access.
cards.citation: Agent identity concepts in Microsoft Foundry (agent-identity) · outline 3.1

cards.q: An insurer already runs an Azure API Management instance and wants to reuse it as the AI Gateway for a Foundry resource. In the Foundry portal under Manage then AI Gateway, the admin chooses Use existing, but the instance does not appear in the list even though she is an Owner on it. Which requirement is the most likely blocker?
options: The API Management instance is not on one of the v2 tiers
The API Management instance has no Application Insights diagnostic setting enabled
The Foundry projects have not yet been added to the gateway
The API Management instance lacks a validate-azure-ad-token inbound policy
cards.answer: The API Management instance is not on one of the v2 tiers
cards.why: Eligibility for reuse requires the instance to be in the same tenant and subscription as the Foundry resource, be reachable from the portal, carry at least API Management Service Contributor, and be created on a v2 tier; with Owner already held, the tier is the remaining candidate. Not having added projects is the plausible distractor, but that only leaves a project's gateway status disabled after the gateway exists, it does not hide the instance from the picker. Diagnostic settings and token validation policies matter for logging and managed identity auth, not for listing.
cards.citation: Configure AI Gateway in your Foundry resources (enable-ai-api-management-gateway-portal) · outline 3.1

cards.q: A media company enables the AI services threat protection plan in Defender for Cloud on the subscription hosting its Foundry workloads. The SOC complains that alerts arrive with the offending prompt text masked, which slows triage. What should be changed, and where?
options: Turn on user prompt evidence in the AI services plan settings under Environment settings for that subscription
Turn on data security for AI interactions so Microsoft Purview can classify the prompts
Turn on AI model security so scanned model metadata is attached to alerts
Add the UserSecurityContext parameters to the application's Azure OpenAI calls
cards.answer: Turn on user prompt evidence in the AI services plan settings under Environment settings for that subscription
cards.why: With the plan on but prompt evidence off, Defender keeps analysing prompts and responses for detection while masking the content in alerts, and the fix is the plan component toggle reached from Environment settings, subscription, AI services, Settings. Enabling data security for AI interactions is the closest wrong option: it is a genuine toggle in the same pane, but it hands prompts to Purview for classification and compliance under a separate Purview licence, and it does not unmask alert evidence. UserSecurityContext adds end-user and application identity to alerts, a different gap.
cards.citation: Defender for Cloud AI services threat-protection onboarding (ai-onboarding) · outline 3.1

cards.q: A pharmaceutical company's Foundry agent summarises supplier documents retrieved through SharePoint grounding. Red teaming shows that hidden instructions inside a retrieved document steer the agent before anyone sees the answer. Which guardrail control stops that content from reaching the agent's memory?
options: An indirect attack control with the annotate and block action at the tool response intervention point
A user prompt attack control with the annotate and block action at the user input intervention point
A groundedness control at the output intervention point
A spotlighting control at the tool call intervention point
cards.answer: An indirect attack control with the annotate and block action at the tool response intervention point
cards.why: Tool response is the intervention point that scans the payload a tool sends back before it enters the agent's memory or reaches the user, and indirect attack is the risk that covers instructions smuggled inside retrieved content. The user input option is the near miss: prompt attack detection at user input catches jailbreak text the human typed, which is not where this payload arrives. Groundedness and spotlighting are both preview risks that are not applicable to agents, so controls built on them simply do not take effect there.
cards.citation: Guardrails and controls overview and Intervention points in Microsoft Foundry (guardrails-overview, intervention-points) · outline 3.1

cards.q: A utility's cloud security lead opens the Data and AI security dashboard, hosted in Defender for Cloud, expecting the AI closer look section to summarise sensitive findings and grounding exposure. The tiles are largely empty despite the AI services plan being on. What is the most likely missing prerequisite?
options: The Defender CSPM plan with its sensitive data discovery extension is not enabled on the subscription
The subscription has not been registered to the Microsoft.Security resource provider
The account lacks the Security explorer role needed to read assessments
Defender for Storage has not been enabled, so grounding data sources are unscanned
cards.answer: The Defender CSPM plan with its sensitive data discovery extension is not enabled on the subscription
cards.why: Full dashboard content depends on Defender CSPM together with the sensitive data discovery extension, alongside the Storage, Databases, and AI threat protection plans, and without CSPM the discovery and sensitive-data views have nothing to draw on. Resource provider registration is the closest wrong answer and is genuinely required, but a missing registration tends to break the dashboard wholesale rather than leave the AI section thin while the plan reports as on. A missing role would block reading assessments entirely rather than selectively.
cards.citation: Defender for Cloud Data and AI security dashboard (data-aware-security-dashboard-overview) · outline 3.1

cards.q: It is 02:10. A payments company's Copilot Studio support agent is, right now, pasting fragments that look like connection strings into outbound replies. Defender is raising near-real-time alerts on every occurrence, but nothing is being stopped. The default real-time protection rule is the only rule in place. What contains this fastest?
options: Create a custom real-time protection rule scoped to that agent with the secret exfiltration detection type, which blocks matching actions before they execute
Edit the built-in Default rule to change its action from audit to block for all agents
Disable prompt evidence collection so the leaked secrets stop appearing in alert evidence
Query the BehaviorInfo table and build a custom detection rule from the matching behaviours
cards.answer: Create a custom real-time protection rule scoped to that agent with the secret exfiltration detection type, which blocks matching actions before they execute
cards.why: The Default rule audits everything and never stops an action; blocking comes only from custom rules, which you create for high-confidence threats and scope to specific agents, exactly the shape of this incident. Editing the Default rule is the closest wrong move: the built-in rule exists to give visibility before enforcement, and blocking is expressed by creating custom rules rather than by flipping the default's action globally. Turning off prompt evidence hides the evidence rather than the leak, and a custom detection rule from BehaviorInfo is after-the-fact hunting, not containment.
cards.citation: Defender real-time protection for AI agents (ai-agent-real-time-protection) · outline 3.1

cards.q: A published Foundry agent application at a shipping line is actively issuing damaging write calls into a partner booking system, and the same application serves two other tenants. The Entra administrator on call is a Global Administrator, and the resource owners are not answering at this hour. What is the correct containment step?
options: Stop the agent application's deployments, then notify the resource owners
Delete the agent application so no deployment can restart, then notify the resource owners
Block the agent in the Microsoft 365 admin center so it disappears from Teams and Copilot
Wait for a resource owner to respond before taking any infrastructure action
cards.answer: Stop the agent application's deployments, then notify the resource owners
cards.why: For an active security threat the guidance is to act first and notify afterwards, and stopping is the reversible infrastructure action for an agent application: it deallocates the compute and the application rejects requests across every channel, while the application and its deployments survive for later restart. Deleting is the closest wrong answer and the most tempting under pressure, but it is permanent, it removes deployments, and it hits every consumer of a multitenant agent with no way back. A Block action in the admin center only affects projection into Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot, leaving the agent fully functional through its own endpoint and APIs.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra agent infrastructure governance (govern-agent-infrastructure-entra-admin) · outline 3.1

cards.q: Defender for Cloud fires a suspected wallet attack volume anomaly on a hotel chain's Foundry resource: one project's traffic is running far above its historical pattern and is starving two other projects of model capacity while the bill climbs by the hour. AI Gateway is already enabled on the resource. What is the containment move?
options: Set a tokens-per-minute limit and token quota on that specific project, since AI Gateway limits apply per project
Remove the offending project from the gateway so its traffic stops routing through API Management
Delete the AI Gateway and the underlying API Management instance to halt all model traffic
Upgrade the API Management instance from Basic v2 to Premium v2 to absorb the request volume
cards.answer: Set a tokens-per-minute limit and token quota on that specific project, since AI Gateway limits apply per project
cards.why: AI Gateway sits between clients and model deployments with limits applied at project level, which is exactly the multi-team token containment case: cap the runaway project and the others regain capacity. Removing the project from the gateway is the nearest wrong answer and is actively harmful, because disabling a project stops its traffic routing through the gateway and therefore removes the only place the limits could be enforced. Deleting the gateway punishes every project, and buying a larger tier funds the attack rather than containing it.
cards.citation: Configure AI Gateway in your Foundry resources and Alerts for AI services (enable-ai-api-management-gateway-portal, alerts-ai-workloads) · outline 3.1

cards.q: During a live investigation at a health insurer, an agent is misbehaving and the SOC needs to know whether it can run without human approval and whether it holds write access to core claims systems, before deciding how hard to intervene. Where in the Microsoft Defender portal does that context live?
options: The agent's risk indicators on the AI agents inventory under Assets, which flag conditions such as privileged business-system access
The security recommendations tab, since recommendations are the definitive statement of an agent's risk level
The incident graph, which computes the agent's risk level from correlated alerts
The Real-time protection rules page, where each rule's scope lists the agents it covers
cards.answer: The agent's risk indicators on the AI agents inventory under Assets, which flag conditions such as privileged business-system access
cards.why: Risk indicators are security conditions derived from configuration, tools, access, runtime activity, and active alerts, and indicators like privileged business-system access or an agent that runs without human approval are exactly what tells you the blast radius before you act. Security recommendations are the closest wrong answer: they are calculated separately from the risk level, so a high-risk agent may carry none at all, and reading them alone understates exposure. The incident graph shows relationships between entities but does not compute agent posture, and the rules page only shows what a rule covers.
cards.citation: Defender AI agent posture risk assessment (ai-agent-risk-assessment) · outline 3.1

cards.q: After a week of Copilot surfacing an HR investigation file to the wrong readers, a county council pauses to harden before restarting rollout. Remediating permissions across the affected sites will take a month. What should have been in place on day one to keep Copilot away from those sites while the permission work runs?
options: SharePoint Restricted Content Discovery on the affected sites, so they are excluded from Copilot discovery during remediation
Retention policies that delete content unaccessed for three or more years on the affected sites
An auto-labeling policy applying a sensitivity label to the unlabeled sensitive files
Removal of every sharing link on the affected sites through item-level remediation
cards.answer: SharePoint Restricted Content Discovery on the affected sites, so they are excluded from Copilot discovery during remediation
cards.why: Restricted Content Discovery is the interim guardrail for precisely this window: it exempts sites from Copilot while access and permissions are being fixed, and it is removed once remediation lands. Auto-labeling is the closest wrong option and belongs in the same protect flyout, but labels only reduce exposure once a matching restrict-by-label policy exists, and applying labels does not itself take the site out of Copilot's reach. Retention deals with stale content, and stripping sharing links is called out as an action to use sparingly because it blocks legitimate access and forces owners to rebuild it.
cards.citation: Purview DSPM data risk assessments and Microsoft 365 Copilot data-foundation guidance (dspm-oversharing, configure-secure-governed-data-foundation) · outline 3.1

cards.q: A brewery's AI administrator is writing the standing procedure for agent incidents after a messy week. She wants the runbook to state plainly what a Block action in the Microsoft 365 admin center actually achieves, so nobody again believes an agent was neutralised when it was not. Which statement belongs in the runbook?
options: Block only removes the agent's projection into Microsoft 365 Copilot and Teams; the agent keeps running in Foundry and through its APIs
Block takes the agent's endpoint offline across every channel, so it is equivalent to disabling the agent in Foundry
Block deallocates the compute behind the agent application's deployments and stops charges
Block revokes the agent identity's role assignments, so downstream tool calls start failing
cards.answer: Block only removes the agent's projection into Microsoft 365 Copilot and Teams; the agent keeps running in Foundry and through its APIs
cards.why: Block and Unblock in the Microsoft 365 and Teams admin centers affect agent visibility to users in those specific channels and touch no Azure resource, which is why they are a poor containment action on their own. Equating Block with Disable is the nearest wrong statement and the exact confusion that caused the messy week: disabling a Foundry agent takes the endpoint offline so it rejects requests across Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Foundry, and APIs. Deallocating compute describes Stop on an agent application, and nothing about Block touches RBAC.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra agent infrastructure governance (govern-agent-infrastructure-entra-admin) · outline 3.1

cards.q: A grocery retailer runs its loyalty-points engine on Dsv5 VMs. An auditor notes that card-adjacent data lands on the temporary disk and in the OS and data disk caches, and demands those be encrypted at rest and encrypted in flight to storage. The platform team also refuses anything that burns guest CPU, because the engine is already near its compute ceiling. Which disk protection do you turn on?
options: Encryption at host on the VMs
Azure Disk Encryption using BitLocker inside the guest
Double encryption at rest on the managed disks
Server-side encryption with a customer-managed key through a disk encryption set
cards.answer: Encryption at host on the VMs
cards.why: Encryption at host extends server-side encryption so that the temporary disk, the ephemeral OS disk and the caches on OS and data disks are encrypted on the Azure host and travel encrypted to the storage service, and it consumes no VM CPU. Azure Disk Encryption is the nearest wrong answer: it does cover temp disk and caches, but it runs BitLocker or DM-Crypt inside the guest and therefore does use the VM CPU, which is exactly the constraint given. Plain server-side encryption with a customer-managed key never reaches temp disks or caches, and double encryption at rest adds a second infrastructure layer to persisted disks without solving the cache or temp-disk gap.
cards.citation: Overview of managed disk encryption options and Server-side encryption of Azure Disk Storage (Azure Virtual Machines docs) · outline 3.2

cards.q: A hospital trust is replacing its jump-box estate. Clinical-systems engineers must reach VMs over RDP and SSH, the information governance board requires a recorded audit trail of every administrative session, and the network team has a standing rule that no component in the clinical virtual network may hold a public IP address. Which Azure Bastion deployment satisfies all three?
options: Bastion Premium SKU deployed as private-only
Bastion Standard SKU with shareable links disabled and diagnostic logs sent to Log Analytics
Bastion Basic SKU with an NSG blocking inbound 443 from the internet
Bastion Developer SKU, which uses a shared pool and needs no public IP
cards.answer: Bastion Premium SKU deployed as private-only
cards.why: Session recording and private-only deployment, which removes the requirement for a public IP on the bastion host, are both Premium-only features. Standard is the closest wrong choice because it carries the advanced connectivity features such as native client, custom ports and shareable links, but it records nothing and still requires a public IP address. Basic cannot do either, and stripping inbound 443 from a Basic host simply breaks it; Developer needs no public IP but is a shared, non-production offering with no recording, no peering and one VM at a time.
cards.citation: Choose the right Azure Bastion SKU and About Azure Bastion configuration settings (Azure Bastion docs) · outline 3.2

cards.q: A university builds a new research virtual network and the Bastion deployment fails. The engineer created a subnet named BastionSubnet with a /27 prefix, placed a spare network interface in it for testing, and attached a dynamic Basic public IP. She wants Standard SKU with host scaling later. What must she correct before the deployment will succeed and scale?
options: Rename the subnet to AzureBastionSubnet, resize it to /26 or larger, empty it of other resources, and use a Standard static public IP
Keep the /27 subnet but add a route table sending 0.0.0.0/0 to the Azure Firewall, and convert the public IP to Standard dynamic
Rename the subnet to GatewaySubnet, resize to /26, and delegate it to Microsoft.Network/bastionHosts
Leave the subnet as is and deploy Bastion into the hub virtual network instead, relying on peering to reach the research VMs
cards.answer: Rename the subnet to AzureBastionSubnet, resize it to /26 or larger, empty it of other resources, and use a Standard static public IP
cards.why: Bastion at Basic SKU and above requires a dedicated subnet named exactly AzureBastionSubnet, sized /26 or larger for host scaling, holding no other resources, in the same virtual network as the host, plus a Standard static public IP. The nearest wrong option keeps the /27 and adds routing: a /27 deployed today is rejected, and forced tunnelling all egress through a firewall does not fix a naming or sizing fault. GatewaySubnet belongs to virtual network gateways, not Bastion, and while hub deployment with peering is a legitimate topology it does not repair the malformed subnet she has built.
cards.citation: About Azure Bastion configuration settings, subnet and public IP requirements (Azure Bastion docs) · outline 3.2

cards.q: A car-parts manufacturer enables just-in-time machine access in Defender for Cloud. Most plant VMs appear under Configured, but the twelve VMs sitting behind the shared Azure Firewall all land in the Unsupported group. Those VMs are Resource Manager deployments with network security groups attached, and the firewall is administered centrally through Azure Firewall Manager policies. What explains it, and what do you change?
options: Just-in-time access does not support VMs protected by an Azure Firewall governed by Azure Firewall Manager, so the firewall must be configured with classic rules instead of firewall policies
The VMs lack a public IP address, so just-in-time has no inbound rule to close, and each VM needs a Standard public IP before it can be enrolled
Defender for Servers Plan 1 is enabled rather than Plan 2, and just-in-time becomes available on those VMs once the plan is upgraded
The plant subscription is missing the Microsoft.Security resource provider registration, which blocks creation of the just-in-time network access policy
cards.answer: Just-in-time access does not support VMs protected by an Azure Firewall governed by Azure Firewall Manager, so the firewall must be configured with classic rules instead of firewall policies
cards.why: Just-in-time can program network security groups and Azure Firewall rules, but the firewall must be using Rules (Classic); firewalls controlled by Azure Firewall Manager policies are explicitly out of scope, which is why only those twelve VMs are unsupported. The plan-tier option is the nearest trap: Plan 2 genuinely is a prerequisite for just-in-time, but if the plan were wrong every VM in the subscription would be affected, not only the ones behind that firewall. Just-in-time works over private addressing and needs no public IP per VM, and a missing provider registration would break the whole feature rather than a subset.
cards.citation: Understand just-in-time virtual machine access and Enable just-in-time access (Defender for Cloud docs) · outline 3.2

cards.q: A logistics operator builds a hardened Windows Server golden image in its own datacentre, installs the Azure Connected Machine agent, runs azcmagent connect to confirm it works, then clones two hundred depot servers from that image. In Azure Arc only one machine object appears, its status flaps between Connected and Disconnected, and the depot servers log HTTP 429 responses. What is the correct remediation?
options: On each cloned server run azcmagent disconnect with the force-local-only switch, then run azcmagent connect again so every machine registers under its own unique Arc resource
Raise the Arc resource limit on the resource group, because the default 800 instances per resource group has been exhausted by the clones
Install the Azure Monitor Agent extension on each clone so heartbeats are sent through Azure Monitor rather than the Connected Machine agent
Delete the Arc machine resource in Azure and let the agents re-register automatically at their next five-minute heartbeat
cards.answer: On each cloned server run azcmagent disconnect with the force-local-only switch, then run azcmagent connect again so every machine registers under its own unique Arc resource
cards.why: Connecting the golden image baked the Azure resource identity into the image, so every clone heartbeats against the same resource and gets throttled with 429 responses; the supported fix is a local forced disconnect on each clone followed by a fresh connect with an appropriate credential. The resource-limit answer is the plausible trap: Arc-enabled servers and their extensions have no per-resource-group instance cap, and the 800 limit applies to Azure Arc Private Link Scope resources, not machines. The Azure Monitor Agent does not carry Arc registration heartbeats, and deleting the Azure object leaves the duplicated identity on all two hundred disks.
cards.citation: Overview of Azure Connected Machine agent, cloning guidelines and service limits (Azure Arc-enabled servers docs) · outline 3.2

cards.q: A regional bank has three hundred on-premises Windows and Linux servers in its own datacentre. The security architect wants the full Defender for Servers Plan 2 feature set on them, specifically file integrity monitoring, operating system baseline assessment against the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark, and periodic OS update reporting. Which onboarding path does she choose?
options: Onboard the servers as Azure Arc-enabled machines, then enable Defender for Servers Plan 2 on the subscription that holds them
Onboard the servers directly to Defender for Cloud through Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, then enable Defender for Servers Plan 2
Install the Azure Monitor Agent on each server and connect it to a Log Analytics workspace with the Defender for Servers solution attached
Create an AWS or GCP connector in Defender for Cloud and register the datacentre subnets through the multicloud connector
cards.answer: Onboard the servers as Azure Arc-enabled machines, then enable Defender for Servers Plan 2 on the subscription that holds them
cards.why: Arc gives each on-premises server an Azure resource identity, which is what the Plan 2 features that depend on Arc need: file integrity monitoring, MCSB operating system baseline assessment and periodic OS update reporting are all tied to machines onboarded through Arc. Direct onboarding via Defender for Endpoint is the nearest wrong answer because it genuinely works and delivers the Plan 1 EDR-centred capabilities, but most Plan 2 functionality is unavailable on directly onboarded machines. The Log Analytics agent and Azure Monitor Agent path is no longer how Defender for Servers collects machine data, and cloud connectors cover AWS and GCP estates, not a private datacentre.
cards.citation: Overview of Defender for Servers, Plan Defender for Servers deployment, Enable Defender for Endpoint integration (Defender for Cloud docs) · outline 3.2

cards.q: An insurance company enables Defender for Servers Plan 2 and, within a day, sees the EDR configuration issues recommendation raised against its virtual machines, with findings about antivirus being partially configured and scans older than seven days. No new extension was deployed to the affected VMs that week. Which mechanism produced these findings?
options: Agentless machine scanning, which reads a snapshot of each running VM disk and evaluates the Defender for Endpoint configuration out of band
The Defender for Endpoint sensor reporting live antivirus telemetry into Defender for Cloud through the MDE.Windows and MDE.Linux extensions
The Azure Machine Configuration extension evaluating a guest assignment against the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark antivirus baseline
File integrity monitoring, which watches Defender for Endpoint registry and configuration paths for unauthorised change
cards.answer: Agentless machine scanning, which reads a snapshot of each running VM disk and evaluates the Defender for Endpoint configuration out of band
cards.why: Agentless scanning is what Defender for Cloud uses to assess EDR settings, which is why the checks for stale full and quick scans, outdated signatures and disabled or partial antivirus appeared without any new agent being pushed. The Defender for Endpoint sensor is the nearest wrong answer: it certainly exists on those machines and supplies alerts and vulnerability data, but the EDR configuration recommendations in Defender for Cloud come from the agentless assessment, not from the sensor. Machine Configuration evaluates guest baselines rather than EDR posture, and file integrity monitoring is opt-in and reports file change events, not scan age.
cards.citation: Assess Defender for Endpoint EDR settings and Investigate Defender for Endpoint misconfiguration recommendations (Defender for Cloud docs) · outline 3.2

cards.q: A media broadcaster turns on agentless scanning under Defender for Servers Plan 2. Every VM reports software inventory and vulnerabilities except the editorial cluster, whose managed disks are encrypted with customer-managed keys held in a key vault that uses Azure RBAC for its data plane. Those VMs return no scan results at all. What do you configure?
options: On the key vault, give the Defender for Cloud Servers Scanner Resource Provider identity the Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User role
Switch the editorial disks from customer-managed keys back to platform-managed keys, because agentless scanning cannot read CMK-encrypted disks
Add a key vault access policy giving the VM system-assigned managed identities get, wrap and unwrap permissions on the encryption key
Move the key vault into the same resource group as the disk encryption set and enable purge protection
cards.answer: On the key vault, give the Defender for Cloud Servers Scanner Resource Provider identity the Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User role
cards.why: Agentless scanning supports CMK-encrypted Azure disks, but the scanner needs key permissions to make a secure copy: on an RBAC-enabled vault that means the Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User role for the Defender for Cloud Servers Scanner Resource Provider, and on a policy-based vault the equivalent get, wrap and unwrap permissions. The access-policy option is the closest miss because it names the right three operations but assigns them to the wrong principal, the VMs' own identities, which already have what they need to boot. Reverting to platform-managed keys is unnecessary and destroys the control the broadcaster wanted, and vault placement or purge protection has no bearing on scanner access.
cards.citation: Enable agentless machine scanning and Agentless machine scanning permissions (Defender for Cloud docs) · outline 3.2

cards.q: An energy utility must place Secure Boot and a virtual TPM under every SCADA-adjacent Windows VM so Defender for Cloud can attest boot integrity. Twenty of the VMs are Generation 1, built years ago, and all of them are protected by Azure Backup using a Standard policy. What sequence gets them to an attestable state?
options: Upgrade the Generation 1 VMs to Generation 2 with the Trusted launch security type, migrate their backups to the Enhanced policy, then enable Secure Boot, vTPM and integrity monitoring
Redeploy each VM onto a confidential VM size so the disk encryption keys bind to the TPM, which supplies Secure Boot and vTPM implicitly
Enable the Guest Attestation extension on the existing Generation 1 VMs, which installs a software TPM and starts boot integrity reporting
Change the security type of the Generation 1 VMs to Trusted launch in the VM Configuration blade while they are running, then reboot them
cards.answer: Upgrade the Generation 1 VMs to Generation 2 with the Trusted launch security type, migrate their backups to the Enhanced policy, then enable Secure Boot, vTPM and integrity monitoring
cards.why: Trusted launch is a Generation 2 capability, Generation 1 VMs have a supported upgrade path to Generation 2 with Trusted launch, and a VM protected by a Standard backup policy cannot take the Trusted launch security type until its backup is migrated to the Enhanced policy. The last option is the nearest trap because changing the security type in Configuration is the right portal gesture for an existing Generation 2 VM, but the VM must first be stopped and deallocated, and these are Generation 1 in any case. Confidential VMs are a different, more restrictive family aimed at in-use protection, and the Guest Attestation extension reports on Secure Boot and vTPM rather than providing them.
cards.citation: Trusted Launch for Azure virtual machines, Enable Trusted launch on existing Gen2 VMs, Boot integrity monitoring overview (Azure Virtual Machines docs) · outline 3.2

cards.q: A public transport authority assigns a built-in machine configuration policy to audit TLS settings across four hundred Azure VMs and one hundred and twenty Arc-enabled depot servers. The Arc servers report compliance within the hour. Every Azure VM stays stuck showing no guest assignment data at all. What is missing on the Azure VMs?
options: The Azure Machine Configuration extension together with a system-assigned managed identity, both of which are required on Azure virtual machines
The Azure Connected Machine agent, which must be installed on Azure VMs so they present the Microsoft.HybridCompute resource type to the policy
A Log Analytics workspace association, because guest assignment results are written to the workspace before Azure Policy reads them
The Microsoft.GuestConfiguration resource provider registration, which is never registered automatically for Azure virtual machines
cards.answer: The Azure Machine Configuration extension together with a system-assigned managed identity, both of which are required on Azure virtual machines
cards.why: Azure VMs need the machine configuration extension to pull guest assignments and a system-assigned managed identity to authenticate to the machine configuration service; Arc-enabled servers already carry that capability inside the Connected Machine agent, which is exactly why the depot servers reported and the Azure VMs did not. Installing the Connected Machine agent is the nearest wrong option and is actively unsupported, because the agent refuses to install on an Azure VM. Machine configuration results flow to the machine configuration resource provider and on to Azure Resource Graph rather than to a workspace, and the provider registers itself when policy is assigned through the portal or when the subscription is onboarded to Defender for Cloud.
cards.citation: Azure Machine Configuration prerequisites and What is Azure Machine Configuration (Azure Policy machine configuration docs) · outline 3.2

cards.q: It is 02:10 and a building society's payment VMs are shutting down one after another. Minutes earlier, a session using a stolen operator credential disabled the RSA key in the key vault that backs the disk encryption set for those disks. Disk reads are already failing on the survivors. You have revoked the attacker's session. What do you do right now to bring the estate back?
options: Enable the key again in the key vault, or point the disk encryption set at a new key, then start the affected VMs
Rotate the disk encryption set to a fresh key version and wait for the re-wrap to propagate to every disk and snapshot
Detach the OS disks and reattach them to replacement VMs configured with platform-managed keys
Restore the VMs from the most recent restore points, which were taken before the key was disabled
cards.answer: Enable the key again in the key vault, or point the disk encryption set at a new key, then start the affected VMs
cards.why: When the customer-managed key behind a disk encryption set is disabled, deleted or expired, the dependent VMs shut down automatically and disk I/O starts failing, and they will not boot again until the key is re-enabled or a replacement key is assigned, so restoring key availability is the containment move. Rotating to a new key version is the nearest wrong answer because rotation is the correct hygiene control in peacetime, but re-wrapping data encryption keys does nothing while the referenced key is still disabled, and it does not restart the stopped VMs. Detaching disks to platform-managed keys is not a live operation on encrypted disks, and restoring from restore points rebuilds machines that still point at the same disabled key.
cards.citation: Server-side encryption of Azure Disk Storage, full control of your keys (Azure Virtual Machines docs) · outline 3.2

cards.q: Defender for Cloud is firing brute-force and suspicious sign-in alerts against a university's grading server. A contractor approved a just-in-time request forty minutes ago for RDP with allowed source set to any address, and the three-hour window still has more than two hours to run. An active RDP session is established from an address in a country the university does not operate in. What contains this fastest?
options: Remove the just-in-time allow rule from the network security group now and terminate the established session on the VM
Let the just-in-time window expire so Defender for Cloud restores the network security group to its previous state
Edit the just-in-time policy to shorten the maximum request time and restrict allowed source IPs for port 3389
Disable the contractor's account in Microsoft Entra ID so the request cannot be renewed
cards.answer: Remove the just-in-time allow rule from the network security group now and terminate the established session on the VM
cards.why: Just-in-time opens a temporary allow rule and restores the network security group when the window closes, but connections that are already established are not interrupted, so waiting is not containment. Letting the window expire is the nearest wrong answer precisely because it feels like the designed behaviour: it closes the door for new connections in two hours while leaving the intruder inside. Editing the policy and disabling the account are both correct follow-up hardening and identity moves, but neither cuts the live session or the rule that is admitting traffic right now.
cards.citation: Understand just-in-time virtual machine access and Enable just-in-time access (Defender for Cloud docs) · outline 3.2

cards.q: A pathology lab's imaging VM, a Trusted launch machine with Secure Boot, vTPM and the Guest Attestation extension, has just raised a Defender for Cloud attestation failure alert. The attested boot log deviates from the trusted baseline and the change window shows no approved patching. The VM is still serving requests. What is the containment move?
options: Treat the VM as compromised, isolate it from the network, and rebuild it from a restore point taken before the deviation
Reinstall the Guest Attestation extension so the platform recomputes a fresh baseline from the current boot state
Disable Secure Boot on the VM so it can boot cleanly, then suppress the attestation alert while you investigate
Enable file integrity monitoring on the VM so the changed boot components are recorded for the investigation
cards.answer: Treat the VM as compromised, isolate it from the network, and rebuild it from a restore point taken before the deviation
cards.why: A boot log that deviates from the trusted baseline can mean untrusted modules were loaded and the operating system is compromised, which is exactly the bootkit and rootkit case Trusted launch exists to surface, so isolation and rebuild from known-good state is the response. Reinstalling the extension is the nearest wrong option because it looks like a benign repair, but rebaselining against a possibly tampered boot chain destroys the very signal that fired. Disabling Secure Boot makes attestation fail legitimately and blinds you further, and file integrity monitoring is a useful control to have had in place beforehand rather than a containment action once the boot chain is already suspect.
cards.citation: Trusted Launch with Defender for Cloud, boot integrity monitoring (Azure Virtual Machines docs) · outline 3.2

cards.q: A pharmaceutical manufacturer's Arc-enabled domain controllers are being targeted. An attacker holding a subscription Owner role has already removed an Azure Policy assignment and is now pushing a custom VM extension to the Arc machines, which would run as Local System on Windows. Cloud-side guardrails have not held. What stops the extension from executing on those servers?
options: Configure an extension allowlist on the Connected Machine agent, or disable the extension manager entirely, using azcmagent on each server
Assign an Azure Policy deny rule for Microsoft.HybridCompute machine extensions at the management group above the subscription
Remove the Arc machine resources from Azure so the servers have no resource to receive an extension request
Rotate the service principal secret that was used to onboard the servers to Azure Arc
cards.answer: Configure an extension allowlist on the Connected Machine agent, or disable the extension manager entirely, using azcmagent on each server
cards.why: The Connected Machine agent carries local security controls that take precedence over cloud-side restrictions, which is the designed answer to a legitimately privileged Azure account being abused: an extension allowlist or a disabled extension manager cannot be overridden from the portal. The management-group deny policy is the nearest wrong choice and is good practice, but it is another cloud-based restriction the same over-privileged identity path is already defeating, and policy changes take effect on evaluation rather than instantly. Deleting the Arc resources destroys your visibility and management path mid-incident, and rotating the onboarding secret does not touch an attacker who is acting through Azure, not through the onboarding credential.
cards.citation: Security overview for Azure Arc-enabled servers, agent services and extension manager (Azure Arc-enabled servers docs) · outline 3.2

cards.q: After an incident, a telecoms operator audits its Defender for Servers Plan 2 coverage and finds a set of VMs with no vulnerability findings at all: several use Ultra Disk and Premium SSD v2 volumes, a batch cluster is deallocated outside business hours, and a legacy group carries a tag that the platform team once added to an agentless scanning exclusion list. What is the right hardening response?
options: Rely on agent-based Defender Vulnerability Management through the Defender for Endpoint sensor for those machines, and review the exclusion tags in the agentless scanning configuration
Turn off the individual agentless capabilities that cannot handle those disk types, leaving software inventory scanning enabled for the rest
Increase the agentless scan frequency below twenty-four hours so the batch cluster is scanned during its running window
Migrate the affected volumes to Premium SSD v1 and remove the tags, so that agentless scanning becomes the single source of coverage
cards.answer: Rely on agent-based Defender Vulnerability Management through the Defender for Endpoint sensor for those machines, and review the exclusion tags in the agentless scanning configuration
cards.why: Agentless scanning has real boundaries: VMs on Ultra Disk or Premium SSD v2, machines that are powered off at scan time, and machines matching an exclusion tag are simply skipped, so coverage for those has to come from the agent-based path that the Defender for Endpoint integration already provides, alongside a review of who set the tags. Changing the schedule is the nearest wrong answer because it sounds operational, but the agentless scan runs on a fixed, non-configurable twenty-four hour cycle. Individual agentless capabilities cannot be turned off one by one, and re-platforming production storage to suit a scanner is a disproportionate response when a supported second scanning path exists.
cards.citation: Agentless machine scanning prerequisites and exclusions, plus Defender Vulnerability Management scanning (Defender for Cloud docs) · outline 3.2

cards.q: A national retailer's post-incident review finds that a hardening setting on its till servers was reapplied by the platform team three times in six weeks and drifted back each time, because an application installer reset it. The setting is delivered by a machine configuration policy whose assignments currently report NonCompliant and stay that way. Which change stops the drift from persisting between reviews?
options: Set the machine configuration assignment type to ApplyAndAutoCorrect so the local service returns the machine to the desired state at the next evaluation
Set the machine configuration assignment type to ApplyAndMonitor so the configuration is applied and then watched for change
Set the Azure Policy assignment enforcement mode to Enabled so the platform blocks any deployment that would reset the setting
Add a deny policy on the till servers' resource group so the application installer cannot modify operating system settings
cards.answer: Set the machine configuration assignment type to ApplyAndAutoCorrect so the local service returns the machine to the desired state at the next evaluation
cards.why: Continuous remediation is exactly the ApplyAndAutoCorrect assignment type: when the machine drifts, the agent inside the machine corrects it at the next evaluation rather than waiting for a human. ApplyAndMonitor is the nearest wrong answer and is the default behaviour they already have: it applies once, then reports NonCompliant on drift and leaves it there, which is precisely the pattern the review found. Azure Policy enforcement mode governs whether the policy effect is applied to resources at all, not whether guest settings are self-healing, and a deny policy operates on Azure resource operations and cannot stop an installer running inside the guest.
cards.citation: Remediation options for machine configuration and What is Azure Machine Configuration, enforcement modes (Azure Policy machine configuration docs) · outline 3.2

cards.q: A regional hospital group runs three AKS clusters for its patient-portal microservices. Defender for Containers is enabled on the subscription and the security team already sees cluster inventory, node vulnerability findings and control-plane alerts such as an exposed Kubernetes dashboard. What they never see is any alert about a process that was not part of the image starting inside a running pod. The platform lead asks what is missing.
options: The Defender sensor is not deployed to the clusters, so no sensor-based runtime detections such as binary drift are produced
Agentless discovery for Kubernetes has not been enabled, so Defender cannot read the cluster configuration
The Azure Policy add-on for Kubernetes is missing, so admission requests are not evaluated
Defender CSPM is not enabled, so attack path analysis cannot correlate the runtime signals
cards.answer: The Defender sensor is not deployed to the clusters, so no sensor-based runtime detections such as binary drift are produced
cards.why: Defender for Containers splits its capabilities: posture, image vulnerability assessment and control-plane threat detection are agentless, while runtime threat detection inside the workload needs in-cluster components, specifically the Defender sensor DaemonSet that collects process and network telemetry with eBPF. Binary drift detection and antimalware are named sensor-based capabilities. The nearest wrong option is the Azure Policy add-on, which is real and is deployed alongside Defender, but it is an admission controller extending Gatekeeper that evaluates API requests before they are persisted, so it would block a privileged pod at creation time rather than alert on an unexpected process in a container that is already running.
cards.citation: Microsoft Defender for Containers introduction and architecture, Defender for Cloud docs · outline 3.3

cards.q: A grocery retailer keeps a golden base image in Azure Container Registry that has not been pushed or pulled since a platform freeze five months ago, and it is not running anywhere. A critical OpenSSL CVE is published. The registry is covered by Defender for Containers vulnerability assessment, but the image still shows the findings it had months ago. A security analyst wants current findings for that image today.
options: Pull the image from the registry, which reactivates scanning so the image is included in the daily rescan cycle
Re-tag the image in the registry, because tag changes force an immediate rescan of the underlying manifest
Turn on registry access again in the Defender for Containers plan, because it lapses for idle repositories
Enable agentless scanning for machines, because registry images are only rescanned through node disk snapshots
cards.answer: Pull the image from the registry, which reactivates scanning so the image is included in the daily rescan cycle
cards.why: Registry vulnerability assessment rescans daily only images pushed in the last 30 days, pulled in the last 30 days, or currently running in a monitored Kubernetes cluster. An image outside all three sets simply stops receiving updated findings, and Microsoft's stated remedy is to pull it, which reactivates scanning. Re-tagging is the closest wrong answer because tags do feel like a registry change, but Defender tracks the image manifest and tag operations are not the documented trigger; deleting a tag does not even necessarily delete the manifest.
cards.citation: Vulnerability management for containers, Defender for Cloud docs · outline 3.3

cards.q: A retail bank is retiring client secrets from its AKS Standard payment services. The team enables the OIDC issuer and workload identity on the cluster, creates a federated identity credential on a user-assigned managed identity, annotates the service account with the client ID, and redeploys. Tokens are acquired fine at first, but after every pod restart the payment pods fail to authenticate to Key Vault. The manifest carries the service account but no other identity-related metadata.
options: Add the pod label azure.workload.identity/use set to true to the pod template spec so the mutating webhook injects the token volume and environment variables
Add a second federated identity credential to the managed identity, because one credential is consumed per pod restart
Assign the pod an Azure Key Vault Secrets User role on the identity rather than on the vault, because the role must follow the pod
Install the Microsoft Entra pod-managed identity add-on alongside workload identity so restarted pods can reach the node identity endpoint
cards.answer: Add the pod label azure.workload.identity/use set to true to the pod template spec so the mutating webhook injects the token volume and environment variables
cards.why: Only pods carrying the azure.workload.identity/use label get mutated by the workload identity admission webhook, which is what injects the Azure environment variables plus the service account token volume that is projected into the containers. Microsoft documents the exact symptom in the question: without the label, AKS moves workload identity to a fail-close behaviour and pods fail after they restart. The nearest wrong option is adding federated identity credentials, which is a real limit worth knowing, but that limit is 20 credentials per managed identity and credentials are not consumed per restart.
cards.citation: Microsoft Entra Workload ID on AKS · outline 3.3

cards.q: A university research platform runs on an AKS Standard cluster with the Azure Policy add-on installed. Deployment Safeguards were switched on last term. A postgraduate group deploys a pod that runs as root with hostPath mounts, and it is admitted without complaint, though warnings appeared in the terminal. The platform team wants that class of workload rejected in the research namespaces while leaving the shared tooling namespace alone.
options: Set the safeguards level to Enforce and set the Pod Security Standards level to Baseline or Restricted, then exclude the tooling namespace
Leave the safeguards level at Warn and rely on the Defender sensor to block the pod once runtime telemetry flags the hostPath mount
Switch the cluster to AKS Automatic so Pod Security Standards default to Restricted for all namespaces
Assign the built-in privileged container policy with an Audit effect and let Defender for Cloud remediate the finding
cards.answer: Set the safeguards level to Enforce and set the Pod Security Standards level to Baseline or Restricted, then exclude the tooling namespace
cards.why: On an AKS Standard cluster the safeguards are opt-in and you choose Warn or Enforce, and Pod Security Standards start at Privileged, which enforces nothing. Denial and mutation only happen at Enforce, and the PSS level has to be raised explicitly with the pss-level setting; namespace exclusions are supported at both levels. Switching to AKS Automatic is the nearest wrong option because Automatic really does ship safeguards in Enforce mode by default, but its PSS default is Baseline rather than Restricted, and rebuilding the cluster mode to change an admission setting is not the control being asked for.
cards.citation: AKS Deployment Safeguards for best-practice enforcement · outline 3.3

cards.q: An automotive parts manufacturer has one Azure Container Registry shared by eleven build pipelines. Every pipeline authenticates with the same registry admin username and password held in a variable group. An auditor points out that all pushes appear in the logs as one identity, and that rotating the credential would break every pipeline at once. The build platform runs on Azure DevOps self-hosted agents on Azure virtual machines.
options: Give each agent virtual machine a managed identity and grant it the least-privileged registry role, then authenticate with az acr login
Keep the admin account but regenerate the second admin password on a schedule so pipelines alternate between the two passwords
Issue each pipeline a repository-scoped token so pushes are attributable and Microsoft Entra RBAC roles can be assigned per repository
Have each pipeline call az acr login with the expose-token option and cache the returned access token as a pipeline secret
cards.answer: Give each agent virtual machine a managed identity and grant it the least-privileged registry role, then authenticate with az acr login
cards.why: Managed identity is the documented unattended path for Azure-hosted CI/CD to reach a registry: no stored credential, per-identity attribution, and Microsoft Entra RBAC roles for pull-only or push. The admin account is explicitly described as a single account per registry with full permissions, designed for one user and not for sharing, and its two passwords exist to allow rotation without downtime, not to make sharing acceptable. Repository-scoped tokens are the nearest wrong option and would improve attribution, but Microsoft states that token-based repository permissions do not support Microsoft Entra RBAC role assignments, which is exactly the governance the auditor wants.
cards.citation: Azure Container Registry authentication with managed identities · outline 3.3

cards.q: A logistics operator must stop its Premium container registry from being reachable from the open internet. The registry is consumed by one AKS cluster behind a Standard load balancer and by a fleet of build servers with fixed public addresses. A network engineer adds IP rules for the build servers and sets the registry default action to Deny, but AKS image pulls start failing intermittently the next morning.
options: The cluster egress address is not fixed by default, so either control cluster egress to a known address or reach the registry through a private endpoint
IP access rules are ignored for AKS because the kubelet authenticates with a service principal rather than a client IP
The registry needs public network access disabled as well, because IP rules only take effect once the public endpoint is turned off
The IP rules exceeded the 40 rule limit for a registry, so the later rules covering the cluster were silently dropped
cards.answer: The cluster egress address is not fixed by default, so either control cluster egress to a known address or reach the registry through a private endpoint
cards.why: Microsoft calls this out directly: an AKS cluster does not have a fixed outbound address by default, so a registry restricted to specific IPs may reject it, and the fix is to control egress traffic for the Standard load balancer or to move to Private Link, where IP rules do not apply at all. Disabling public network access is the nearest wrong option and sounds like more security, but it overrides all firewall configuration and would break the build servers too; and it would also cut virtual network access if the registry uses a service endpoint. A registry supports up to 200 IP access rules, so the limit answer is simply wrong.
cards.citation: Configure public IP network rules for Azure Container Registry · outline 3.3

cards.q: An insurer exposes twelve HTTP-triggered functions in one function app. A partner integration needs to call exactly one of them, a quote-callback endpoint. The integration team asks for a key and the operations engineer is about to copy the value shown on the App keys page of the function app.
options: Issue a function key created on the Function keys tab of that one function, because function keys are scoped to a single function endpoint
Issue the default host key from the App keys page, because host keys can be revoked per caller without affecting other functions
Issue the _master key so the partner can also call the runtime REST APIs if the callback needs replaying
Issue a system key, because extension-scoped keys are the supported way to authorize a single webhook-style endpoint for a partner
cards.answer: Issue a function key created on the Function keys tab of that one function, because function keys are scoped to a single function endpoint
cards.why: Functions access keys come in scopes: a function key authorizes only one function endpoint, a host key authorizes every function endpoint in the app, and the master key additionally grants administrative access to the runtime REST APIs. Handing over the host key shown on App keys is the nearest wrong option, and it is exactly the trap here, because that page is where the engineer was already looking, but it would grant the partner every other endpoint in the app. System keys are real but are created only by specific extensions for internal callers such as an Event Grid subscription, and their values cannot be set by you.
cards.citation: Work with access keys in Azure Functions · outline 3.3

cards.q: A housing charity runs a Consumption logic app whose Request trigger receives case referrals from a partner agency. Today the partner calls the trigger URL with its shared access signature query parameters. Compliance wants callers authenticated by Microsoft Entra ID instead, with no callable URL secret in circulation. The integration developer defines an authorization policy on the logic app resource with Issuer and Audience claims and tells the partner to send a bearer token.
options: Also disable SAS authentication on the trigger, because a Consumption workflow endpoint should use only one authorization scheme
Leave SAS enabled as a fallback, because Azure Logic Apps evaluates the Entra policy first and only falls back if no token is present
Replace the authorization policy with a managed identity on the logic app, because inbound calls are authorized by the workflow identity
Move the authorization policy to the Request trigger itself, because resource-level policies apply only to outbound HTTP actions
cards.answer: Also disable SAS authentication on the trigger, because a Consumption workflow endpoint should use only one authorization scheme
cards.why: For Consumption workflows, a request-based trigger endpoint accepts exactly one inbound authorization scheme, Microsoft Entra OAuth 2.0 or SAS. Enabling one does not switch the other off, and using both at once produces an error because the service cannot choose, so the correct completion is to disable SAS and restrict authorization to Entra. The nearest wrong option is leaving SAS as a fallback: there is no documented precedence between the two schemes, and leaving the SAS keys live keeps the callable-URL secret in circulation, which was the compliance objection. Standard workflows behave differently and may combine other authentication types with SAS still enabled.
cards.citation: Azure Logic Apps workflow access and data protection · outline 3.3

cards.q: A fashion retailer publishes its storefront through Azure Front Door Premium with a WAF policy in front. Penetration testers show that the App Service origin still answers directly on its azurewebsites.net hostname, letting them bypass the WAF entirely. The app is on a multitenant App Service plan, not an App Service Environment, and must stay reachable through Front Door.
options: Add a site access restriction rule allowing the AzureFrontDoor.Backend service tag and filtering on the X-Azure-FDID header value of that profile
Add an IP-based access restriction rule listing the virtual network address ranges used by the Front Door profile
Enable App Service authentication with a Microsoft Entra provider so unauthenticated origin requests are rejected
Add a service endpoint access restriction rule for the subnet that hosts the Front Door origin group
cards.answer: Add a site access restriction rule allowing the AzureFrontDoor.Backend service tag and filtering on the X-Azure-FDID header value of that profile
cards.why: Service tag rules filter inbound traffic to well-known Azure service ranges, and App Service supports HTTP header filtering on any rule, with X-Azure-FDID documented for identifying a specific reverse proxy instance. Combining them is the named use case, because the service tag alone would still admit any customer's Front Door profile. The nearest wrong option is an IP-based rule: Microsoft states that these rules cover virtual network ranges only when the app runs in an App Service Environment, and Front Door does not present a stable customer-owned range in the multitenant service. Enabling authentication protects the application session but does not stop the origin from being reached around the WAF.
cards.citation: Azure App Service access restrictions · outline 3.3

cards.q: A media startup deploys eight container apps into one Azure Container Apps environment. The images sit in a private Azure Container Registry, and the deployment YAML currently holds the registry admin username and password as a Container Apps secret. The database connection string is also a plain Container Apps secret. The new head of platform wants both credentials off the app definition before the next release.
options: Assign a managed identity for the registry image pull with the AcrPull role, and replace the connection string with a Key Vault secret reference
Move both values into environment variables on the container app so they are no longer stored in the secrets store
Enable the Container Apps token store, which caches registry and backend credentials in Blob Storage on the app's behalf
Create a repository-scoped registry token for image pull and mount the connection string as a secret volume
cards.answer: Assign a managed identity for the registry image pull with the AcrPull role, and replace the connection string with a Key Vault secret reference
cards.why: Container Apps documents managed identity image pull as the pattern that avoids registry administrative credentials and gives fine-grained access through the AcrPull role, and its secrets guidance is to avoid holding production secrets in Container Apps directly and to use Key Vault references instead. The nearest wrong option is the token store, which is a genuine Container Apps feature but stores end-user authentication tokens in Blob Storage for the built-in auth flow; it has nothing to do with registry or database credentials. Moving secrets into plain environment variables makes the exposure worse, not better.
cards.citation: Security overview for Azure Container Apps and Managed identities in Azure Container Apps · outline 3.3

cards.q: It is 09:40 on a Monday and the hospital's patient-portal WAF on Application Gateway is blocking clinicians. Since a rule set upgrade an hour ago, every appointment-notes submission returns 403.
