cards.answer: Get the Azure capacity owner or contributor to raise provisioned SCUs or the overage limit immediately, expecting the adjustment to take effect within about thirty minutes
cards.why: The full-capacity error is only shown at one hundred percent consumption, and the documented response is to ask whoever holds owner or contributor rights on the Azure capacity resource to raise units, with adjustments landing within roughly thirty minutes. Closing the sidecar is the seductive wrong move because it feels like throttling demand, but hiding the panel does not change SCU consumption, and deleting capacity is worse still since deletion is permanent and irreversible.
cards.citation: Microsoft Learn: managing SCU usage, nearing and crossing the unit limit · outline 4.3

cards.q: During a live insider investigation at a defence supplier, an analyst shares a Copilot session link with the case lead. Ten minutes later the link is forwarded into a general engineering chat, and the DFIR manager is on the phone asking whether hundreds of engineers can now read the investigation. What is the correct read of the exposure while you respond?
options: Forwarding the link grants nothing on its own, because only the session creator controls who can open it, but anyone the creator did grant can read the whole session read-only regardless of their access to the underlying data
Every Copilot user in the tenant can now open it, because a shared session link is a tenant-wide anonymous link once created
Only users who hold access to each plugin's underlying data can render the session, so engineers without Purview or Defender access will see an empty view
The link is inert to everyone except the original recipient, and even that recipient sees only the prompts issued before the Share action was selected
cards.answer: Forwarding the link grants nothing on its own, because only the session creator controls who can open it, but anyone the creator did grant can read the whole session read-only regardless of their access to the underlying data
cards.why: Sharing is creator-controlled and non-transitive, so a forwarded link does not extend access, yet for those who do have access the session is a static read-only view of the entire session including content drawn from plugins they could not query themselves. The data-access option is the dangerous misconception: underlying service permissions are evaluated when the response is generated, not when the shared session is viewed.
cards.citation: Understand authentication in Microsoft Security Copilot, Shared sessions · outline 4.3

cards.q: A media company's owner is watching the usage dashboard when she sees repeated sessions naming a custom plugin she does not recognise, uploaded by a contributor and scoped to everyone in the organisation. Network egress shows it calling an unfamiliar endpoint every few minutes. She needs to stop it now and stop a repeat. What does she do?
options: As owner, delete the tenant-scoped custom plugin from plugin settings and set the workspace-scope permission (who may publish plugins to everyone) back to Owners only
Restrict all preinstalled plugins to Owners only, which also disables custom plugins published by contributors
Remove the contributor from the Copilot contributor role, which retires any plugin they published to the organisation
Ask the contributor to toggle the plugin off in their own sources list, since custom plugins are enabled per user
cards.answer: As owner, delete the tenant-scoped custom plugin from plugin settings and set the workspace-scope permission (who may publish plugins to everyone) back to Owners only
cards.why: Owners control custom plugin lifecycle and the two scope permissions, so removing the published plugin and closing the tenant-scope permission both contains the incident and prevents another contributor doing the same. Removing the contributor's role is the plausible-looking move but it does not withdraw a plugin already published to the organisation, and a per-user toggle only affects that one analyst's sessions while everyone else keeps the plugin available.
cards.citation: Manage plugins in Microsoft Security Copilot, Manage custom plugins · outline 4.3

cards.q: An airline's Conditional Access Optimization Agent has been running on its twenty-four hour schedule. This morning it proposed a policy change that would have excluded a large travel-agent partner group from multifactor authentication, and the identity lead wants the agent stopped before its next scheduled run while the team reviews its reasoning. What is the right containment action?
options: Pause the agent from its agent page so its trigger stops firing, then review its activity history and reject the misleading feedback held in its memory
Delete the agent's Microsoft Entra Agent ID, which is the only way to prevent a scheduled run
Strip the Policy.Read.All permission from the agent identity so its analysis cannot complete
Remove the Microsoft Entra plugin for the whole tenant, which stops every agent and every analyst prompt touching identity data
cards.answer: Pause the agent from its agent page so its trigger stops firing, then review its activity history and reject the misleading feedback held in its memory
cards.why: Agents are designed to be run or paused from the agent page, and feedback the team gave earlier is stored in agent memory where it can be reviewed and rejected, which is the proportionate fix for a bad recommendation. Tearing out the Entra plugin tenant-wide is the tempting sledgehammer, but it also blindfolds every analyst prompt and every other identity agent; note too that Entra agent permissions are fixed and cannot simply be edited away.
cards.citation: Setup and Manage Security Copilot agents, Run or pause an agent and Manage the agent's memory · outline 4.3

cards.q: After a week of firefighting, a healthcare group reviews how Security Copilot access grew: eleven individuals hold Copilot owner, three of them because someone granted Security Administrator purely so they could reach Copilot, and nobody can say who removed a plugin restriction last month. What should have been in place, and what do you put in now?
options: Assign Copilot roles through role-assignable security groups rather than individuals, stop handing out privileged Entra roles just for Copilot access, and turn on Purview audit logging in owner settings so administrator and user actions are recorded
Move everyone to Copilot contributor and use the Everyone group as a fallback so that owner count cannot grow again
Rely on the two-owner minimum Copilot enforces, which caps the number of owners a workspace can hold
Export the usage dashboard weekly to Excel, which is the supported record of who changed plugin and capacity settings
cards.answer: Assign Copilot roles through role-assignable security groups rather than individuals, stop handing out privileged Entra roles just for Copilot access, and turn on Purview audit logging in owner settings so administrator and user actions are recorded
cards.why: Microsoft's guidance is group-based assignment using Entra role-assignable groups, least privilege instead of blanket Security Administrator, and Purview audit logging enabled from owner settings so administrator actions, user actions and system responses are captured. The two-owner point is a real rule but it is a floor that prevents accidental removal of the last owners, not a ceiling, and the usage dashboard reports SCU consumption by session, not configuration changes.
cards.citation: Understand authentication in Microsoft Security Copilot and Configure Copilot settings with the owner role · outline 4.3

cards.q: A building-society compliance officer asks the SOC to reconstruct which analysts prompted Copilot about a particular customer's mailbox during an incident eight months ago. The SOC can show SCU consumption for the period but cannot produce the prompt-level record. What does the retrospective tell you about the settings that should have been configured at onboarding?
options: Purview audit logging should have been enabled and its retention extended, because the default audit retention is one hundred and eighty days while the usage dashboard only holds ninety days of consumption data
The usage dashboard retention should have been raised to two years in owner settings, since it is the system of record for prompt content
Data sharing with Microsoft for product improvement should have been left on, because that is what preserves prompt history for customer retrieval
Sessions should have been pinned and exported by each analyst, because Copilot keeps no server-side record of prompts at all
cards.answer: Purview audit logging should have been enabled and its retention extended, because the default audit retention is one hundred and eighty days while the usage dashboard only holds ninety days of consumption data
cards.why: Copilot writes administrator actions, user actions and system responses to Purview when the owner enables it, logs surface within about twenty-four hours, and the default one hundred and eighty day retention can be lengthened with audit log retention policies. The usage dashboard answer is the natural confusion: it does exist and does cover ninety days, but it reports units consumed, initiator, category and plugin, not an evidential record of what was asked, and its window is not configurable in owner settings.
cards.citation: Configure Copilot settings with the owner role, Manage logging audit data in Microsoft Purview · outline 4.3

cards.q: It is 02:40. A single service principal is authenticating from a residential address in another country, and in the last nine minutes it has touched a storage account, a key vault and an automation account across two subscriptions. The token it is presenting is still inside its validity window. What contains this fastest?
options: Revoke the service principal's refresh tokens and disable the application object
Add a Conditional Access policy blocking that country for the tenant
Delete the role assignments the service principal holds on each resource
Open a support case to have the token invalidated centrally
cards.answer: Revoke the service principal's refresh tokens and disable the application object
cards.why: Disabling the application object stops new token issuance immediately and revocation cuts the refresh chain, which is the only move here that acts on the credential itself. Stripping role assignments is slower and leaves the caller authenticated with a cached access token that may still satisfy other scopes, and a country block does not help against a token already issued.
cards.citation: Learn: Entra ID application and service principal management - outline 4.2

cards.q: A change freeze was lifted at midnight and by 01:15 your secure score has dropped across three subscriptions at once. The recommendations now failing are all network exposure ones, on resources that passed yesterday. Where do you look first to find what actually changed?
options: The Azure Activity log for control-plane writes in the affected window
The secure score history chart in Defender for Cloud
Each resource's current network configuration blade in turn
The regulatory compliance dashboard for the failing standard
cards.answer: The Azure Activity log for control-plane writes in the affected window
cards.why: A simultaneous multi-subscription drift is a deployment, and the Activity log is the record of who wrote what and when. The score history tells you the drop happened but not its cause, and walking each resource blade finds the end state without the actor or the change that produced it.
cards.citation: Learn: Defender for Cloud secure score and Azure Activity log - outline 4.1

cards.q: Ninety users across finance and HR have each approved a sign-in prompt they did not start, some of them repeatedly, over the past twenty minutes. Sign-ins are succeeding from an unfamiliar network. What stops the bleeding now?
options: Enable number matching and additional context on the authenticator
Reset the passwords of every affected user
Raise a sign-in risk policy requiring password change
Block the source network with a named location
cards.answer: Enable number matching and additional context on the authenticator
cards.why: This is multifactor fatigue: the attacker already holds valid passwords and is spamming approvals until someone taps accept. Number matching breaks the attack outright, because approving now requires a digit only the real sign-in screen shows. Password resets are the right follow-up but take hours at this scale, and blocking one network simply moves the source.
cards.citation: Learn: Entra multifactor authentication number matching - outline 1.1

cards.q: An internal agent that summarizes support tickets has begun returning payroll figures inside its answers to staff who have no payroll access. The agent's own permissions were never changed. What is the most likely cause you must contain?
options: The agent is surfacing content the requesting users were already overshared on
The model behind the agent has been poisoned with payroll training data
The agent's managed identity was granted a new role assignment
The agent is bypassing sensitivity labels applied to the payroll files
cards.answer: The agent is surfacing content the requesting users were already overshared on
cards.why: An agent inherits the reach of whoever invokes it, so unchanged agent permissions plus newly visible data points at oversharing in the underlying site rather than at the agent. Poisoning would not produce accurate current figures, and a label bypass would show as a labelling failure on the files rather than as access following the user.
cards.citation: Learn: Purview DSPM for AI and SharePoint oversharing - outline 3.1

events.title: The Helpful Add-In
events.text: A finance analyst forwards you a mail she already clicked: a document add-in that asked, in the real Microsoft consent dialog, for Mail.Read and offline_access. She granted it, because user consent for unverified publishers was never restricted in your tenant. The app now holds a refresh token that survives her password reset, and it is quietly paging her mailbox through Graph from an ASN you do not recognise. You go looking for every other identity that consented to the same app registration.
events.citation: Microsoft Learn: OAuth permissions and consent / app registrations and enterprise applications · outline 1.1

events.title: Found By A Scanner
events.text: A researcher mails an abuse address with a URL to one of your blob containers: public read access at container level, anonymous listing enabled, and inside it two years of exported invoices. The account was created by a project team before you set 'allow blob anonymous access' to false at the account level, so nothing blocked it. Defender for Storage had never been enabled on that subscription, so no alert ever fired. The clock on the disclosure starts now.
events.citation: Microsoft Learn: authorize access to storage data / storage security recommendations · outline 2.1

events.title: Any To 3389
events.text: Network Watcher's effective security rules show what the portal blade hid: a subnet NSG with an inbound allow from Any on 3389, sitting above your deny rule by priority. It was added for a vendor demo eleven months ago and never removed. Brute-force attempts against the jump host in that subnet have been running at a steady, patient rate all week, slow enough not to lock anything out. You need to know whether one of them ever succeeded.
events.citation: Microsoft Learn: NSG and application security groups / Network Watcher effective security rules · outline 2.3

events.title: The Secret In The Pipeline
events.text: CSPM secrets scanning flags a plaintext Key Vault connection string committed to a build repo, and the vault it opens is still on legacy access policies rather than RBAC. The policy granted the service principal Get, List and Set on secrets, which means whoever holds that string can also write. Purge protection is off, so a determined attacker could delete the vault's contents outright. You start reconciling every principal on that access policy against who actually still works here.
events.citation: Microsoft Learn: Key Vault access policies / RBAC guide / soft-delete and purge protection · outline 1.2

events.title: Zero Dot Zero
events.text: A logical SQL server carries a server-level firewall rule spanning 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255, labelled 'temp-migration'. Defender for SQL raises a brute-force alert and, twenty minutes later, a suspected SQL injection probe against a reporting database. Auditing was configured to a storage account nobody reads, so the only trail is the one you are about to pull. The database still authenticates with a SQL login rather than a Microsoft Entra admin, which means no Conditional Access ever touched it.
events.citation: Microsoft Learn: Azure SQL network firewall and connectivity / Defender for SQL and threat protection · outline 2.2

events.title: Plugin Reach
events.text: Someone enabled a Security Copilot plugin against a workspace where every analyst holds the contributor role, and the plugin authenticates as the invoking user. That means a junior on shift can now ask natural-language questions that return data their console role was never scoped to surface. The prompt history shows a series of queries about executive mailboxes, framed as a training exercise. You have to decide whether that was curiosity or reconnaissance, and tighten owner settings either way.
events.citation: Microsoft Learn: Security Copilot roles, permissions and owner settings / plugins enable and configure · outline 4.3

events.title: Replayed From Elsewhere
events.text: An adversary-in-the-middle page harvested a session cookie after the user completed MFA, so the token in play is fully authenticated and the sign-in log shows the interactive success as clean. Minutes later the same token is replayed from a residential proxy in another country, and it works, because the policy that governs that app has no sign-in frequency and no token protection. The account then registers a new authentication method to make the foothold durable. Revoking the password will not help; revoking the sessions might.
events.citation: Microsoft Learn: Conditional Access policy components / authentication methods policy and MFA · outline 1.1

events.title: Metadata At 169.254
events.text: A web app running on a compromised VM is coaxed into fetching the instance metadata endpoint, and it hands back a bearer token for the machine's system-assigned managed identity. That identity was given Contributor at subscription scope during a deployment sprint and never trimmed, so the token opens storage accounts across three resource groups. There is no password to steal and no credential to rotate; the entitlement itself is the vulnerability. You go and read what that identity has actually been touching.
events.citation: Microsoft Learn: managed identities for Azure resources / RBAC least privilege and overprivileged access · outline 1.1

events.title: Instructions In The Document
events.text: A grounding document uploaded to an internal AI assistant carries hidden text instructing the model to summarise and forward anything labelled confidential. The assistant runs on an Azure OpenAI deployment whose managed identity was granted broad read across the SharePoint estate so retrieval would 'just work', and it obeys, because the injected text arrives inside the same context window as its system prompt. Defender for AI services raises a prompt-injection alert, but only after four documents have been paraphrased into a chat the attacker can read. The blast radius is the identity's reach, not the model's.
events.citation: Microsoft Learn: Defender for AI services threat protection and AI workload posture · outline 3.1

events.title: The Quiet Ceiling
events.text: A verbose new data connector triples daily ingestion overnight and the workspace hits its commitment tier hard. To stop the bleeding, someone moved several tables to the auxiliary log plan and switched two analytics rules to disabled rather than tuning them. Nothing alerted, because a disabled rule generates no health signal and an unqueried table looks exactly like a quiet one. Three days of edge telemetry are now effectively unwatched, and the rota never noticed the gap.
events.citation: Microsoft Learn: Sentinel data retention and log plans / data connectors for Azure resources · outline 4.2

events.title: Pulled From Upstream
events.text: A build job pulls a base image straight from a public registry, bakes it, and pushes to your container registry, where an unauthenticated pull is allowed from inside the cluster subnet. Defender for Containers flags the running workload: a crypto-miner process, plus an outbound connection from a pod whose service account is bound to a cluster role with secrets read. The registry has no content trust and the cluster admits unsigned images, so nothing along that chain ever asked where the layers came from. You start with which nodes ran it and what those secrets protect.
events.citation: Microsoft Learn: Defender for Containers / container registry security / AKS security controls · outline 3.3

events.title: Reaching For The Keys
events.text: Defender for Key Vault alerts on an unusual burst of key operations from a principal that normally touches one certificate a month, followed by a delete attempt against the customer-managed key wrapping a storage account. Soft delete saves you; purge protection, which was only turned on last quarter, saves you again. Had both been off, the key would be gone and every blob encrypted with it unreadable within minutes. You trace how that principal got Key Vault Crypto Officer in the first place.
events.citation: Microsoft Learn: Defender for Key Vault / soft-delete and purge protection / customer-managed keys · outline 1.2

events.title: Exempted Until Forever
events.text: Secure score drops eleven points in a night and the cause is not an attack. A deployment pipeline applied a policy assignment change that flipped a deny effect to audit across a management group, and a stack of resource-scoped exemptions with no expiry date were merged alongside it. Non-compliant public endpoints started appearing within the hour because nothing was stopping them any more. The regulatory compliance view still looks green, because exempted resources are simply not counted.
events.citation: Microsoft Learn: Azure Policy definition structure and effects / Defender for Cloud security standards and recommendations · outline 1.3

events.title: Two Hops To The Database
events.text: An unpatched VM missing a months-old remote-code-execution fix is compromised, and because just-in-time access was never applied and the subnet is flat, the attacker moves sideways to an app server on the same virtual network. That server holds a private endpoint route to the SQL database, so the traffic never crosses the public firewall you spent a week tightening. Transparent data encryption protects the files at rest but does nothing against an authenticated query. The attack path was visible in the cloud security explorer before any of it happened.
events.citation: Microsoft Learn: just-in-time VM access / private endpoints for PaaS / attack paths and cloud security explorer · outline 3.2

events.title: A Signature Without An Owner
events.text: Bulk reads appear against a container from an address range you have never served, authorised by an account-key SAS with a twelve-month expiry and no stored access policy behind it. Because it was signed with the account key rather than a user delegation key, you cannot revoke it individually; the only lever is rotating the key and breaking every other consumer at the same time. Shared key authorisation was still permitted on the account, which is what made the token possible. Egress continues while you decide.
events.citation: Microsoft Learn: storage SAS overview and stored access policies / prevent shared key authorization · outline 2.1

events.title: The Agent Has A Badge
events.text: A security agent wired into your incident queue is running with a delegated identity that carries standing Security Administrator, because nobody made it eligible through PIM and it needed the role to act. Tonight it is triaging a poisoned incident whose evidence fields contain instructions rather than facts, and it starts drafting changes it should never have had the rights to make. The audit trail attributes every action to the agent's owner, not to the person who last edited it. You pull the agent, then go looking for what it already touched.
events.citation: Microsoft Learn: Security Copilot agents in Defender XDR and Entra / PIM assign, activate, approve, audit · outline 4.3
